en: *Shangsheng jing ruisheng chao*, Scroll One, compiled by the Bhikṣu Shouchian of Longxing Monastery in Zhending Prefecture.
As for these topical headings (*ke*), they are fundamentally intended to distinguish categories of meaning; one must recognize their sequential gradations. For example, it is like arranging them...
In taking refuge, it is essential to know the source from which one is born. As for its name, it originally exists to distinguish it from others and prevent confusion;
thus, one should understand its additions as being like the continuation of branches and leaves, allowing one to see both their connection and their separation, as is the case here.
Regarding the title of the sub-commentary (*śāstra*), excluding the volume number, there are four stages. First is the correspondence between the exegesis and the subject to be explained:
the first eleven characters constitute the subject to be explained, which already possessed this name even before the sub-commentary existed; thus, this constitutes the first stage.

The single character "sub-commentary" (*shu*) is the exegesis itself, for a sub-commentary is so called because it provides detailed explanations of the meaning. After the sub-commentary was composed, [the following was added...]

Thus its name is established. In this way, one cannot first combine the characters of the *sūtra* with the characters of the commentary (*śāstra*), and then subsequently combine them with the five characters beginning with "contemplation" (*guan*).
Therefore, when providing the explanation, they are connected to the preceding characters; this is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.

Within that which is explained, there is further a second pair of the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*): the first ten characters are the signified, while the single character "sūtra" is the signifier.
This refers to the expressive [words]. Although the substance of this sutra consists of both the expression and the expressed meaning, what is essential lies precisely in hearing it.
Furthermore, among those who provide relative explanations, it is common to emphasize the expressive words while omitting the expressed meaning; this is not contradictory.
These characters precisely represent that which is spoken and that which is heard. Within their names, there is a risk of confusion with various other scriptures;
therefore, the term "that which is expressed" (*so-ch'üan*) has been added to form a single title. This is also analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.

Furthermore, within "that which is expressed," there is a third pair consisting of the subject who contemplates and the object contemplated. While the character "contemplate" (*kuan*) generally applies to both [subject and object], in this title it refers only to the capacity [of the subject].
"Contemplation. The subsequent nine characters refer to that which is contemplated.

Although this sutra also describes the matters of Maitreya’s rebirth above and the celestial palaces, its primary purpose is solely to encourage practitioners of the nine grades to aspire for rebirth.

Therefore, when explaining it, the subject and object of contemplation are inverted to form a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Furthermore, within these nine characters representing the object of contemplation, there is its [first]...
Regarding the four pairs of "producer and produced": the first six characters constitute the producer, while the subsequent three characters constitute the produced.
Alternatively, the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) may be termed the "produced," just as when one arrives at a house, the house is called the "place arrived at.

However, as for the term "deva" (heavenly being), it refers to the luminous purity, sovereignty, and divine efficacy; thus, those who possess contentment are *devas* primarily among sentient beings. This is because—
Regarding the term "named after the receptacle world" (*bhājanaloka*): this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound (possessive determinative) that takes its name entirely from another [term].

Alternatively, the former name for the devas was "Great Contentment" (*tuṣita*), which is a general name for the entire class of devas. Now, this Lord of Devas is born among that multitude; thus, the specific is included within the general, and he is called "born there.
This is also like the meaning of "place of birth" (*upapatti-sthāna*). Here, the designations of "agent" and "object" are established in opposition. This is the title of the present work.
The "Middle and Right" (Zhōngzhèng) clarifies that [the title] can be generated; this is because it causes people to feel joyful attachment toward the Bodhisattva.

For this reason, it may also be analyzed as a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "that which depends on the inverted fall. The preceding explanation was based on proceeding from the outside toward the inside.

If, however, one explains by proceeding from the front toward the back, one may first establish the correspondence between the subject (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), then the generation of the subject and object, then the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*), and finally the explanation of the subject and object. Furthermore, or...
Within that which is capable of producing [the result], a pair is established. To illustrate the function, a person is cited as the counterpart.

Maitreya Bodhisattva cites the person; the term "upper birth" (upapatti) illustrates its function. Since Maitreya is himself a bodhisattva, and the Maitreya Bodhisattva is himself the "upper birth," this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
If one looks toward the three characters "Tuṣita Heaven" below, the order is reversed.
It falls under the category of "dependent on another" (adhīna-svāmika), because Maitreya Bodhisattva of Tuṣita Heaven has been reborn there.
Regarding the other questions concerning these two sets of inversions—both the separations and the combinations—they are all set aside; there remains only their contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

How can this respond to what is expounded in the Sūtra? Answer: The Sūtra’s exposition is complete, explaining both the primary and the secondary. It distinguishes between the separated and the combined to avoid confusion, setting aside the secondary while preserving the primary through the contemplation of the inversions.
Thus, there is no contradiction. Question: The sūtras contain practices of nine grades; where can these be seen within this title? Answer:

They are contained within the character "contemplation" (guān). Question: It may be that focusing the mind on a single object is called contemplation, but how can the cultivation of merit and so forth be termed contemplation?
Answer: Because even when cultivating other practices, one constantly contemplates; therefore, all such practices are collectively termed [contemplation].
"Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). As in the term "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*), the sub-commentary below states: "Taking contemplation as the primary element, they are all termed 'contemplation.

This is also like the names "insight into faith" (*śraddhābhisamaya*) and "insight into precepts" (*śīlābhisamaya*), which are formed through a *sāmīpya* (proximity) compound. In such compounds, the name of another [element] is fully adopted. However, this [present case] primarily concerns the practice of the nine grades;
the name of the practice itself is "correct," with correct observation serving as its auxiliary. This differs from the cases of insight into faith and insight into precepts.
It serves as an aid. Because it aids in attaining the correct name, it is called "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*). Why is this? It is said that there are six kinds of clear realization;
therefore, clear realization is taken as its primary designation. This explains that the cause for producing rebirth is summoned through the attainment of birth.
Nine types of practice are required to correctly summon it; it cannot be summoned by the practice of mere observation alone, nor can such a superior body be produced thereby.

[The Master] asks: Since one has already perceived the causes for its arising within the character "contemplation" (觀), why is it not stated that the practitioner possesses the agent and object [of the action], but rather that the Bodhisattva possesses the agent and object of what is produced?
[The Master] answers: The intent of the sutra is to cause one to contemplate the Bodhisattva, to rejoice in being born together with them, and thereby to create the causes for that birth.
Since that which is produced by the Bodhisattva is precisely that which is produced by the practitioner, there is no need to state it separately.

As for the "creator-cause," it refers to the practitioner’s own body capable of producing [the visualization]. Since this is not a separate category, there is no basis for explaining it separately within the object of contemplation.
Thus, the meaning of the title is fully contained within what is expounded in the sutra and does not contradict it.

Having briefly explained the title of the commentary according to my own understanding above, regarding the various combinations and divisions, there are points that differ from the old interpretations. In...
Those who come to examine this should carefully attend to its rhythm. As for other discrepancies, they shall be distinguished in the main text.
Furthermore, those who compose works according to the *zhī* (branch) tradition write with varying degrees of elaboration and brevity as the occasion demands;

their expansions and contractions are not fixed, being measured against the capacities of their audience and the scope of their own minds. Nevertheless, one must grasp the essential purport, ensuring that the matter remains appropriate. What is to be feared is excess.
How much more so! If one expands too far, one immediately forgets the root; if one contracts too much, it is difficult to understand. Such is the meaning taught in this sutra:

it is nothing other than nature and characteristics, as well as cause and effect. If one were to investigate these by tracing them back through successive stages, the gateways of meaning would be immeasurable.
Even if one exhausted their entire lifespan, one could not reach the ultimate limit of such [teachings], let alone those intended for the sake of rebirth in the heavens. Furthermore, for example:

Regarding the three objects: why is it necessary to discuss what is observed? Why is this so? Because in all such cases as these, one need only know that by practicing the conduct, one will surely attain birth among those [gods].
If one were to follow the explanations in detail, they would extend indefinitely;

fearing that one might thereby lose the opportunity to cultivate the karma for rebirth in the heavens, I have merely followed the commentary to provide a brief outline of the general principles, establishing how one will certainly attain birth through the gradual progression of the nine grades.
This is essential. Let those who come not be held accountable. Question: Placing the title on the exterior allows one to discern the contents quickly without even unrolling the scroll;
the principle here is beyond doubt. Many scriptures have this feature. Furthermore, there are four strokes crossing one another—what do these signify?
Answer: These correspond to three Sanskrit syllables of a *dhāraṇī*. This is translated as "Holding and Turning. [The fourth character is] *Siṃha* (Lion).
Jueyun says: "This means 'to maintain. By practicing according to the sutras, one maintains one's roots of goodness and does not fall into the evil realms.
T'ien-ch'in explains: "This means 'to transform. By practicing according to the sutras, one transforms the mundane into the sacred, transforms the small into the great, and even attains Buddhahood.

This is done collectively to distinguish [these texts] from secular writings. [This is] extracted from the Vinaya texts. Question: Regarding the four categories of sutras, śāstras, commentaries, and sub-commentaries...

Question: Regarding the names and the texts composed [under those names], do they have fixed standards? Answer: Yes. A *sūtra* follows the capacities of sentient beings and accords with their meanings, consisting directly of prose and verse;

it does not further cite other works or interpret the textual meaning of others. A *śāstra*, however, employs logical analysis (*yukti*) to examine the nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Alternatively, he may set forth the scriptural teachings and explain them; for the most part, he does not cite the texts of others to interpret the meaning, but rather provides his own explanations of the textual meaning first, and only then cites others as corroboration.

The term *shu* (commentary) means to comment upon and organize [the text] according to its meaning; it mostly cites passages to explain the meaning, yet it does so by arranging them according to their sequence as topical gates.

The term *chao* (abridgment), however, carries the sense of being incomplete through omissions and brevity; it mostly provides explanations as the occasion demands, failing to reach full completeness.

Thus, it is called "omissions and brevities" (*lou-lüe-bù-bei*). "Omission" (*lou*) means to drop or omit. Because the power of the mind is insufficient, there are things left out; this constitutes laborious effort.

This refers to "humility" (*qián*). Alternatively, "exertion" (*láo*) and "humility" (*qián*) may be distinguished: one exerts oneself because one's strength is insufficient; one is humble because one possesses strength. "Briefly" (*lüè*) means to omit or abbreviate.

"Exertion and humility" are treated similarly; when combined, they do not constitute a complete [explanation]. Alternatively, one may follow one's own capacity, or omit what has already been explained, or what is easily understood—all such cases may be abbreviated.
Furthermore, following the sense of "merely" (*dàn*), it is sufficient to explain only the essential meaning; it is not necessary to provide headings, conclusions, or formal transitions.

[The text is] complete. Regarding the titles established in these commentaries (*śāstra*) and sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*), some are indeed commentaries but are self-humbly termed "sub-commentaries," while others are sub-commentaries but are praised by others as "commentaries.
For example, works such as the *Lüzuàn* (Brief Compilation) call themselves "sub-commentaries" but are praised by others as "commentaries.

Works such as the *Duìfǎ shū* (Commentary on the Abhidharma) are fundamentally "commentaries" but are self-humbly termed "sub-commentaries. Question: What is the difference between "lecturing" (*jiangshuo*) and "explaining the meaning" (*jie shi mingyi*)? Answer:

"Kiang" (講) means to deliberate and measure; "shuo" (說) means to proclaim and express. Characters follow speech, which is emitted from the mouth. "Jie" (解) carries the meaning of escaping and being freed from;
it also means to divide and to open. "Shi" (釋) carries the meaning of removing and shedding;

it also means to depart and to distance oneself. These two names [of the title] do not derive their characters solely from speech; they are manifested through the three karmas [of body, speech, and mind]. They are also named after [the term] "leaving behind enmity" (*li-yuan*), and so forth.
Explanation: Now, within this context, "explanation" does not refer merely to hostility and the like;

rather, it refers to the elucidation of the meaning of the text regarding those points previously not understood, as well as various doubts, obstructions, and challenges. Just as with hostility and the like, these points that were not understood are elucidated by means of this teaching.
The title of the treatise has thus been presented above.

Among personal names, one first cites the basis [of the name]. "Jing" (Capital) means "great. There are four such capitals; here, we take the old Western Capital of Chang'an. It is also a numerical designation.
Because the laypeople residing therein and the number of those in the capital were great, it was used as a name [for the person]. This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (locative compound).
The *Fengsu tong* states: "The Capital was not created by human effort; it is the nature of Heaven and Earth. This is an expression of praise for its excellence.
These words do not concern the meaning of the characters themselves. As for "Daci'en Monastery," it is one of the ten great monasteries of Chang'an.
It was established by Emperor Gaozong to repay the kindness of his compassionate mother who nurtured him.

Regarding the term "si" (monastery), it means "to govern" or "to reach. It is named after the "Honglu Si" (Court of State Ceremonial) among the nine ministries. [The word] "shamon" (śramaṇa) means "one who has ceased [evil]."
"Evil. There are four kinds of it, as fully explained elsewhere. "Compiled" (*zhuàn*) means also "collected" (*jí*). Question: What is the difference between the four terms:

*shuō* (to speak), *zuò* (to create), *shù* (to narrate), and *zhuàn* (to compile)? Answer: *Shuō* refers to oral discourse. *Zuò* refers to the original production; neither of these existed beforehand, hence they are called "speaking" and "creating.

That which exists beforehand is called "narrating" (*shù*), which applies to both that which was originally non-existent and that which was already existent. *Zhuàn* means to collect; it collects old materials to form a work, and thus it is named "collection" (*jí*). In the present age...

Regarding the transmission [of this work]: "compiled" (*zhuan*) is superior to "collected" (*ji*), yet this pertains only to human sentiment and does not concern the literal meaning of the characters. Question: In titles, one speaks of "narrating" (*shu*) when referring to a person, while one speaks of "compiling" (*zhuan*) when referring to a person.

Since these refer to the relationship between the person and the Dharma, why do they appear different? Answer: To describe what existed in the past is "narrating"; to indicate what is produced in the present is "compiling."
If one discusses them in terms of "new" and "old," both exist. Question: According to the current commentary (*śāstra*), how can it be said that there is an "old" version?
Answer: Both originate from other scriptures, or were heard from the accounts of others; thus they are termed "old," but this does not concern the present text itself. Question:

In the case of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Wei-shi shu), where the sūtra and śāstra are paired, or the root text and its commentary are paired, it is called "narrating and composing. As for the commentaries on these treatises, which are old and which are new? Answer: Regarding the sūtras...

Regarding the initial realization, [the *Śāstra*] praises its superiority as being exclusively new; however, the *Treatise* (論) is based on the *Sūtra*, and since it has been so from early on, it is exclusively old. Because the *Treatise* is contrasted with the *Sūtra* to manifest and explain the *Sūtra*, it is termed a "narration" (*shu*). Although it is not the full text, the meaning must necessarily be so. Yet, this is not like a commentary (*shu*) which cites the text to explain the meaning, or which narrates the meanings of others while serving as its own explanation of the text—such cases are instead termed "composition" (*zao*). This is because the original [text] and the commentary are relative to one another, as in: [Text: "The mind is originally pure. [Commentary: "The mind is originally pure; there is no defilement. In such cases, the commentary explains the meaning of the original text. However, the *Śāstra* does not do so; rather, it is a separate work that explains the *Sūtra*. Therefore, it is called a "narration" (*shu*). Furthermore, regarding the term "narration": when one takes the words of another and explains them, it is called a "narration"; when one explains the meaning of the text oneself, it is called a "composition. Thus, although the *Śāstra* is not a "composition," it is certainly not a "narration" in the sense of merely citing and explaining the text. It is simply that the *Śāstra* explains the *Sūtra*, whereas a commentary explains the *Śāstra*. For this reason, it is termed a "narration. Moreover, the *Śāstra* does not cite the *Sūtra* word-for-word; it explains the meaning through the power of its own reasoning. Therefore, it is called a "narration. If one were to cite the text and explain the meaning, it would be a commentary. If one were to explain the meaning of another's text, it would be a composition. Since the *Śāstra* is neither of these, it is termed a "narration. As for the phrase "not like a commentary," it means that a commentary cites the text to explain the meaning, whereas the *Śāstra* does not cite the text but explains the meaning through its own reasoning. This refers to the commentary (*vyākhyā*). Furthermore, its *śāstra* (explanatory treatise) must cite the root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*), because it is intended to explain the meaning of that root treatise.

Question: Regarding the single character "zuàn" (to compile/arrange), does it function as the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*)? Answer: When initially divided into three sections, the term applies solely to the agent who compiles, because it distinguishes between the person and the Dharma.

When divided into two sections, it may be treated as the object being compiled, because it clarifies for whom the Dharma was taught; thus, once the compilation is complete, [the distinction is resolved].

Regarding the title for this Dharma work, I have composed it as a *karmadhāraya* (attributive compound). If one were to take it as referring to the author, it would be a *tatpuruṣa* (appositional compound) with a contradictory sense.

As for the structural divisions of the original draft, there were only three sections; following the precedent of virtuous masters and others, they could be made into two sections. Now, having separately revised and supplemented them, I have combined them into two sections.

I fear that those who do not yet know may be led to understand that such was the case; it is not merely for the sake of making it different from the old version. As for the remaining textual meanings, all...
All have been explained. Although there are two types of praise and censure, I fear they would be too prolix, so I shall cease [further discussion].

Regarding the phrase "To trace the origin" (*yuán fū*): it is the opening of speech and the momentum for entering the text. If one follows the literal meaning, "origin" (*yuán*) means "beginning," and "fū" is a particle.
When one exhausts the purport of the scripture, its beginning is found in *tathatā* (Suchness). From this, it flows forth through successive stages; for this reason, it is called [the "origin"].
The *niṣyanda-dharma* (outflowing True Dharma) and the *svasaṃbhoga-kāya* (body of self-enjoyment) realize the *dharmakāya*.

Once the *dharmakāya* is purified, wisdom manifests the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) as described above to preach this sutra; therefore, it is shown to be all-pervasive and universally encompassing.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the nature and substance are profound and dark," "nature" (*xing*) here refers to the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; "substance" (*zhi*) refers to the essence (*tattva*).

Since True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the essence of all phenomena, it is called "nature and substance. This essence is deep and remote, subtle and difficult to reach, hence it is termed "profound and dark" (*yǎomíng*).
It thus transcends the tracks of hoofprints and is beyond the reach of words, for teachings are like tracks, whereas this [Reality] surpasses all things.

The elephant is not a mundane object because it serves as a metaphor for that which is to be illustrated. Nevertheless, it nonetheless encompasses all phenomena and is the sovereign master of all dharmas.
The former [section] refers to the fundamental nature of reality (*dharmatā*), while the latter pertains to the awakened nature (*bodhi*) as it is to be realized.

This is not merely that which has emerged from the entanglements (*nirmukta-kośa*); the former is also not merely that which remains within the entanglements (*saṃvṛta-kośa*). It is simply contrasted with that which transcends words and is beyond the realm of sensory objects. The above...

It immediately transcends words and images; how could one who has emerged from the bonds (saṃsāra) not be like this? That which is below is not an object for the ears or eyes; how could one still within the bonds perceive it through sight or hearing?
The "above" refers to subsuming the branches back into the root; the "below" refers to [the relationship between] the root and the branches.

Thus, how could this depend on being within or having emerged from the bonds? If one takes the character "awakening" (jue) to mean "emerging from the bonds," is it not because this is the originally awakened nature?

Indeed, it is only at the time of attaining Buddhahood that one becomes the awakened nature (*bodhātman*). It is simply said that upon emerging from the entanglements (*saṃkleśa*), one is designated as the Great Dharmakāya;
it does not mean that one only becomes the awakened nature once one has emerged from the entanglements. Consider this further.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the cloud-like wisdom that pervades the moon of the *ghaṭī*," these four lines below cannot be understood by others.

Of the first two lines, even Bodhisattvas are still deluded regarding the Truth; even in the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), it has not yet been clearly realized. First comes the metaphor, followed by the application to the Dharma. "Pervading" (*fang*) means to compare or extend.
This tenth stage is named the Cloud of Dharma Stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*) because its wisdom is like a cloud. This wisdom of the cloud is called "pervasive wisdom" (*fangzhi*).
"Cloud. It may be explained as follows: "Fang" (方) means "great. Because the wisdom of the Great Dharma is like a cloud, it is called the "Wisdom Cloud.
This is because when this Bodhisattva contemplates True Suchness (Tathatā), it is as if viewing the moon through a thin silk gauze; thus, [the truth] is not yet fully clear.
Because there are still obstructions to the Buddha-ground, one is thus still deluded. Question: For what reason is the wisdom of this ground like a cloud?
There are three meanings: first, it contains all waters; second, it can obscure the void; third, it fills the void. Wisdom also has three meanings:
first, wisdom can contain and store the waters of *dhāraṇī* and so forth; second, wisdom can conceal and cover like the sky.
The two obstacles of grossness and heaviness are as vast as space. Third, wisdom is able to fill all like space;
the qualities upon the wisdom of the dharmakāya are like water, for they pervade everywhere.
Commentary: Regarding the two lines, "Borrowing the blade of wisdom from among the thick bamboos," etc., these two phrases are unfathomable even to the Śrāvakas;

they likewise contain both a dharma and a simile. Even those of sharp faculties do not yet know how to realize them. "Borrow" (jiǎ) means to rely upon, or it may mean to provisionally assume. As for "the blade of wisdom," it is because wisdom is like a blade.
Such people of sharp faculties may either proceed in groups or leap ahead. As for "splitting the bamboo and cutting it," one bamboo [may be split].
It is like this: regarding a great quantity of bamboo, one cannot split it all at once. "Cong" means a thicket; "yun" refers to the bamboo itself.

Now, taking a great quantity of bamboo, one cannot split it with a single stroke. Because *śrāvakas* only realize the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and cannot realize the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), this is what is meant by being "unfathomable" and not being "suddenly severed.
This contrasts with the aforementioned [analogy of] seeing the moon through a fine gauze.
"Clear. Now, this "thicket of bamboos" (*cong yun*) refers to a process that is gradual rather than sudden. *Kui* (to measure) means to gauge; it is largely synonymous with *cha* (to examine).

Both *shen* (spirit) and *ling* (numen) are glossed as "subtle. *Li* (principle) is the ultimate truth. *Ji* (mechanism) refers to the essential point; both terms designate *tathatā* (suchness). The great meaning may thus be understood.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "The ultimate Way is perfected and the pure countenance is revealed," these two subsequent lines indicate the simultaneous realization of the two bodies (*dvikāya*).

The first line refers to the attainment of the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), and the latter line refers to the realization of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Both are obtained because one has reached the perfection of the ultimate Way through liberation.
"Pure" (*chui*) means unadulterated; "countenance" (*rong*) refers to the physical form or deportment. Thus, this [phrase] pertains to its own...

The Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), the Ultimate Reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the True Consciousness (*tathatājñāna*) are all suchness (*tathatā*). When "pure," it is free from entanglements and is therefore the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*).

"Manifesting" means making clear. Once wisdom has been realized and manifested, it is "pure" in the sense of being free from obstructions. Because it is verified by wisdom, it attains the designation of "Dharma Body" through its freedom from obstructions.

Commentary: "Then" means that after having realized the body of true reality (*dharmakāya*), one subsequently manifests a provisional body (*nirmāṇakāya*) according to the capacities of sentient beings.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "looking down to uplift those on the ten stages," the first part clarifies the manifestation of bodies according to capacities, while the latter part clarifies the formal manner of such manifestations.

The former consists of four phrases: two phrases concern the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), and two phrases concern the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). The *saṃbhogakāya* corresponds to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). "Looking down" (*fu*) means descending.
Furthermore, the Buddha dwells above, looking down to receive them and manifesting his Buddha-body. "Sū" (疎) signifies that which can be clearly distinguished or understood.

Although he has personally attained the Dharma-body, it is something people do not understand; therefore, it is called "sū. As for "Hǎimù" (海目), this merely cites his eyes as being like the four great oceans;
there are also features such as eyebrows like the five Mount Sumerus, which are difficult to fully describe in writing. Regarding the term "Bǎofāng" (寶方), it reveals that this is...
The Pure Land is established solely as the true reality. This is because the retribution of others resides exclusively within the Pure Land.

Below, the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is explained. "Kong" means to control; "ti" means to elevate; and "ting" means to emerge. It manifests as a transformation body in order to receive those of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).

Since the transformation body universally benefits the assemblies of the three vehicles, it is like a mountain, for demons cannot move it. Furthermore, it is like Mount Sumeru, for it is most honored and lofty. It frequently dwells therein.

The "defiled land" (*saṃkliṣṭa-bhūmi*) is called a "stained realm. The appearance of hills, mounds, and the like is termed "defiled. This does not pertain to the outflows (*āsrava*). [In the] Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "like a great bell," etc., the preceding part has already been explained according to the Dharma. The following four lines are metaphors. Although there are two distinct matters, both apply to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
The body that manifests is like the bell and like the moon; the body manifested is like the sound and like the shadow. As for this...

The "bell" refers to the manifest body. Internally, it is free from grasping; thus, it is called "empty. Just as a bell cannot produce sound if its interior is not hollow, so too is this true for the actual body.
Its essence is compassion, fundamentally intending to benefit others; in this regard, it is like the bell receiving a strike from the outside, which is termed "reception.
Originally, when it has not yet received a strike, it likewise does not produce sound. This striking is precisely the "trigger" (the condition).
This is the condition for desire. That which is like the moon is the body capable of manifestation; when it is internally free from the two obstacles, it is termed "realization.

Just as if the moon were not clear, there would be no light, so too with the actual body: when it gives rise to the benefit of others, it is like that moon, externally emitting radiance and thereby manifesting its form.
If it does not emit external radiance, the reflection likewise does not appear. Now, to speak briefly again, it is called "emptiness."

It is not a grasping. "Realization" means being free from obstructions; "receiving" means waiting for the capacity [of the recipient]; "radiance" means the manifestation of function. The above has distinguished the manifestor and that which is manifested.
As for the specific nature of the "capacity," it refers to the striking [of the bell] and the purity of the vessel, both of which constitute the capacity. "Striking" is the ripening of the faculties;

"requesting," "waiting for deliverance," and so forth, refer to the purity of the vessel, which is the sentient being who lacks obstructions such as lack of faith. Only when the faculties are ripened and there are no obstructions does [the teaching truly take place].

"Manifestation" (xian) means to appear. "Hong" means great. "Jiao" refers to the bright moon. "Xun" means to follow or accord with. "Si" means to be unrestrained; it carries the sense of letting loose.

Here, it refers to the actual body letting itself loose and manifesting as a provisional body (*upāya-kāya*). Alternatively, one may distinguish this from the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* heaven through two metaphors:
the retribution of that heaven lacks the characteristic of arising from the aggregates (*skandha*), just as sound emerges from a struck bell. This is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The descent into birth and the mothers and so forth are like vessels. Although the vessel is used as a metaphor for the capacity (the *mātr̥kā*), since that capacity includes the mothers and others, they may be distinguished.

[The] *Śū* [commentary] states: "Therefore, there are" [these distinctions]. This follows the previous heading to introduce what follows. Because the two bodies previously mentioned correspond to different capacities, their ritual procedures (*vidhi*) differ;
thus, the two bodies are also distinct. If one relies on the former interpretation, it inherits the teaching of the Dharma from afar; if one relies on the latter interpretation, it is also...
I have recently received your letter.

Regarding the passage beginning with "To propagate and honor [the teachings] as a repayment for the Buddha's grace," the following demonstrates the ritual protocol, which consists of a preliminary exposition followed by a conclusion.

Within the exposition, there are two parts, because each of those two bodies possesses two aspects: the initial and the final. Thus, the text is divided into two sections. Within the section concerning the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) of others, the first is...

Having received the office and attained Buddhahood, he immediately proceeded to his seat to preach the Dharma. This is because there is no place for him to dwell in heaven or to undergo birth in the lower realms.

Within the context of the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), he first dwells in heaven and subsequently descends to be born. The first four lines distinguish the initial characteristics of these two bodies;
each has two lines. "Shao" means to succeed or continue; "long" means flourishing or prosperous. The place where the preceding Buddha attained enlightenment is named [the site of enlightenment].

"To cause to flourish" means to succeed and continue that flourishing; thus it is called "succession and flourishing. As for the term "Jian-tai" (Discerning Terrace), it refers to a terrace-seat made of *vaidūrya* (lapis lazuli) gemstone.
When he received his office, he sat upon this seat, hence it is so named. "Zuan" (to compile/continue) also means to succeed. "Ye" (karma/enterprise) refers to the foundational enterprise;

it is largely the same as "succession and flourishing. "Yi" (to bequeath) means to leave behind. Having departed from the fundamental [form], he manifested [in another state], setting aside his coarse body to respond to those with the karmic capacity.
To encounter [him] is called "leaving behind" (yí). It was his physical body that remained in the Indranīla-maṇi palace in Tuṣita Heaven.
Regarding the character "yí," there is a variant reading "yí" (to transfer/move); examine this carefully.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "consoling the mature roots and hastening to the seat," the following two lines distinguish its subsequent characteristics.

One line concerns the body and one concerns the action. "Consoling" (fǔ) means to take pity upon; "hastening" (qū) means to proceed toward. The Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) does not descend from heaven, but proceeds directly to its seat to attain Buddhahood and preach the Dharma.

The Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is the reverse of this: it descends, which refers to the descent into birth; it leaves traces, which refers to the traces of its activities, such as dwelling in the womb and so forth.
"Characteristics. Because they are all traces.

"Commentary": "This is" (*si nai*)—*si* means "this," referring to the aforementioned forms and appearances; *nai* is a particle used to conclude the preceding statement after the reference has been made.

The concluding phrasing is also distinct; however, it must be understood through implication. The term "three periods" also applies to the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body). "One birth remaining before Buddhahood" (ekajātipratibaddha) also applies to other forms of retribution.
"Mong" means great; "ling" means wondrous. There is no textual passage that speaks of the consecration (abhiṣeka) of the nirmāṇakāya.

Therefore, the statement regarding the assumption of office refers to the retribution received by others. This directly accords with this sūtra’s account of the stage of "one birth remaining" (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
Consequently, what follows merely concludes the discussion of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). This concludes only up to that point;

thus, the subsequent passage states, "Because of the ritual models," which implies that what preceded this was not concluded, as it manifested transformations according to the capacities of sentient beings—this can be understood through careful examination. Alternatively, one may say that while [the manifestation] is proximate, its momentum extends to arise from afar. Question: One...

If one has already been born [in the Pure Land], how can there be the "retribution of another birth" (he-bao)? Answer: According to the *Fayuan zhang*, it exists by way of logical implication (*yi-zhun*), as explained in detail therein;

there is no need to labor over demonstrating it here. Question: At which stage of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is it called "one more birth" (*yisheng*)? Furthermore, what is meant by the "place to be filled"?

Regarding the question of whether one becomes a deva or a human being, the answer is as follows: According to the *Fayuan zhang*, the position of the "Successor" (*kṣetrapūra*) is equivalent to the position of a human being and does not pertain to Tuṣita.
Furthermore, the term "one birth" (*ekajāti*) here does not refer to the body that attains Buddhahood; rather, there is yet another birth required before one finally becomes a Successor.
Within this context, if one speaks in terms of the "great birth," it refers to the Bodhisattva who is about to go to Tuṣita and stand before the Buddha.

The body is designated as "one lifetime. Furthermore, because there are those who come and go between the human and celestial realms, two bases and two intermediate states together constitute one lifetime.

Alternatively, if referring to minor births, this specifically indicates the celestial realm; for the body of a Bodhisattva undergoes only the "lower birth" (descent), as it is the primary basis of the single intermediate state.
When the intermediate and primary bases are spoken of separately, they may be four or two; however, here, based on a single period, they are combined into one and thus called "one."

Question: Since these are all the bodies of bodhisattvas, how do they accord with this Buddha-body? Answer: These are called "transformation bodies" (*nirmāṇakāya*) in contrast to the "retribution body" (*vipākakāya*).
Transformation bodies also possess both cause and fruit; one may mention either according to the context, as it is unnecessary to state them in full.
This principle applies to all such cases, and there is no contradiction.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "As for this present sutra," although the substance of the sutra is twofold, the subsequent praise of its efficacy also encompasses its practice and fruit, as these emerge from the sutra.
Therefore, there are four metaphors, which should be understood in their respective order. Alternatively, within the meaning [of the teaching], practice and fruit are also subsumed;
the abridgment [of other versions] is not superior, so we now take only this one. The teaching is like a single rain, for it can sprinkle everywhere. The principle is like a river. Three...
Because they cross over wild beasts, the six perfections (*ṣaḍpāramitā*) are like a boat, for they transport one across the river. Their fruit is like a chariot, for it draws one out of the house.

Within this fruit there are two: first, the fruit of heaven; second, nirvāṇa. Although the chariot also serves other purposes, it is used here as a metaphor for the fruit simply because it "draws" [one forth].
As for the river, it corresponds to the wild beasts; its meaning lies in the necessity of crossing. While crossing, one is saved; this directly illustrates the meaning of this sutra.

That river lies directly before the boat; one must cross its perilous meaning by means of the boat. This is a metaphor for what is extracted from the sūtras. *Zhen* refers to the horizontal wooden bar at the rear of a carriage.

Now, taking the essential point of the carriage as the subject, a question is asked: "The six practices are like a boat; how do they correspond to the number? Answer: They are spoken of according to their enumeration.

Six constitutes six instances; it does not necessarily mean a single boat. One must grasp the six matters [of practice]; otherwise, there would be nothing but the "superior-of-the-superior" (the ultimate state).
Because they arise [together]. Alternatively, there are six [factors]: the hull, the shape of the boat, the cabin, the oar, the rudder, and the stone at the prow; these constitute the six.
Thus, the six perfections and the six matters are fully set forth, and there is no contradiction.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "Although [the text] probes the profound and elucidates the secret," etc., these four preceding metaphors praise the efficacy of the sutra.

The following passage implicitly addresses potential objections. Within this, there are two parts: first, addressing the objection that the previous section praised only this sutra; second, further addressing the objection that it benefits only those present at one time.
The first part consists of approximately three lines, which itself contains two sections: first, the direct response; second, the explanation thereof. [The Objection: External...
Someone asks: "The four preceding metaphors are all present in various sutras; why do you cite only these and praise them? Or, as an external objection:
"For instance, in sutras such as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Nirvāṇa*, the nature and characteristics [of phenomena] are investigated and cause and effect are discussed at length.
None of these are found within this sutra. How can you use these metaphors to praise it so exclusively? The commentary uses two phrases to refute these points.

The word "although" (sui) contains both gain and loss; it implies both concession and refutation. "To probe" (tan) means to take up. The thread of the sutra passes through the petals of its principles.

Regarding the *Nirvāṇa* and other such texts, though their specific titles differ, the general purport is this: they truly probe the profound nature and characteristics and clarify the secret causes and fruits—this is found in those other *Nirvāṇa* and related sutras.
However, as for rescuing those submerged in the deluge of this degenerate age, [this work alone suffices].
That the mechanism for birth in the heavens arises in accordance with one's disposition exists solely in this sutra; it is for this reason that it is praised so exclusively.
"The trap" (quán) refers to the teaching, used as a metaphor for the instrument by which fish are caught. "Leaves" (yè) refers to the palm leaves upon which the sutra is inscribed.
These, along with the preceding "straw flower," are raised up and displayed in succession.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "Thus the golden light illuminates the evening," etc., the following serves as an explanation and confirmation. How is this known? First, it explains the "rescue from drowning," which refers to the remaining portion of the first practice.
The subsequent scripture describes the emission of light and the manifestation of flowers. The emission of light removes darkness, symbolizing the severing of the causes of darkness (ignorance).
The flowers represent the six practices, symbolizing the future attainment of the fruit. This demonstrates that by relying on this sutra, one easily achieves it; thus, its fruit may be realized.

It is appropriate; therefore, he praises it specifically. As for the power of Maitreya, it is because he does not regress. "External" refers to the first watch of the night. "Candle" (*zhú*) means to illuminate.

"Banner" (*jīng*) means to signify. "Light" (*jǐng*) means clarity. "Retinue" (*tú*) refers to the assembly of followers. "Fragrance" (*fāng*) carries the sense of being aromatic and opening up through analysis.

"Flower" (*wěi*) is simply a blossom. "Before" (*qián*) means in front of one's face. "Confused" (*fēn*) means disorderly. "Deficient" (*kuī*) is synonymous with empty. "After" (*hòu*) refers to what follows.
"Yi" (義) means "fruit" (*phala*).
"Shu" (疏) refers to those such as Miaoxiang and others, who arrived in great numbers. The phrase below, "The Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas," explains that there was a stimulus [for the teaching].
"Wei" (委) means "to go toward" or "to arrive. *Śan wéishí* (善唯識) states it means "succession. They came in succession; here, it may mean "to entrust," as in...
The waves are swift and vast; one relies upon them. When the assembly below gathers, they are like waves and like clouds; thus, this accords with and conforms to such [a state].

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, "Although they received instruction at one time," etc.: the following is the second section, which clarifies that although it only benefits those of one particular time, it does not obstruct [the universal application].
Since the preceding passage merely mentions "those such as Miaoxiang" and "the likes of Śāriputra," an outsider asks:
"If the benefit conferred is thus limited and not extensive, why praise it in such a manner? Furthermore, some may ask: "If the benefit is as described here..."

Regarding the statement "the future world and so forth" in the passage below: the intent of the commentary’s response is that although the initial reception [of the teaching] was narrow, its transmission has become vast;

it is not as if such praise occurred only at a single time. While the capacities of those who received the teaching are listed for only one period, the Sūtra serves as a bridge and raft [for all times].

"Actually reaching a thousand *si* (sacrifices/years). It serves as a ford and a bridge; *si* here refers to the year. Furthermore, it cites "a thousand" as a representative figure, while in reality there were over ten thousand;
the intention is to include what follows, namely the future world. The Xia dynasty called a year a *sui* (age), taking the completion of one cycle of the stars' movement.

It is said that the term *si* was used to denote the completion of one cycle of the four seasons. The Zhou dynasty called it a *nian* (year), taking the time for grain to ripen once. The Tang and Yu dynasties called it a *zai*, taking the [completion of] all things.
Regarding the meaning of "completing a cycle" (*jìnggēngshǐ*): there may be discrepancies in the transmission of the ritual texts, and it is appropriate to follow the character *jì* (cycle).

Taking twelve years as one *jì*, the three periods of the True Dharma (*zhèngfǎ*), the Semblance Dharma (*xiàngfǎ*), and the Final Dharma (*mòfǎ*) together comprise twelve thousand years; this constitutes one thousand cycles.
Now that we have reached the Final Dharma, for over two thousand years, many great benefits have been widely prevalent. How could it be merely a matter of a thousand years?
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "As for the celestial palaces, the sacred realms," and so forth, the following constitutes the commentary on the title of the work.
This is because the title contains the term "Tuṣita," and furthermore, the explanatory text refers to the title as its "counterpart" (*heng*).

Having first separately praised the Tuṣita Heaven, the author subsequently provides a full explanation of the title's text. Upon reaching the section on "Tuṣita," the translation simply stops; this is because it has already been [discussed] previously.
This is because it is a brief praise. The "Celestial Palace" (Tiāngōng) and the "Awakening Garden" (Juéyuàn) both encompass both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings.

Since the palace and the garden both have Bodhisattvas as their presiding deities, they are named after sacred awakening (*śrī-jñāna*). Regarding the term "ornamented by causes" (*yīnyán*): because flowers lead to fruits, they are called "ornaments" based on the causes. "Spirit" (*shén*) means "suchness" (*tathatā*).
A territory belonging to the capital is called the "capital precincts" (*jīngjī*); this should be understood by analogy. "Harmonious" (*xié*) means "to accord."
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva embodies boundless virtues, which are designated as "virtue" (guṇa). Because this virtue traverses the groves and gardens, it is called "Virtuous Treading" (Guṇavati).
Alternatively, "grove" (vana) refers to the exterior, as it is where the Bodhisattva wanders;
"palace" (kūṭāgāra) refers to the interior, as it is his actual dwelling place.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "Not by the pivot of the mind can one grasp and contemplate," the first part briefly praises its excellence, while the latter part demonstrates its inexhaustibility.
The first sentence indicates that the mind’s objects of perception cannot be fathomed; the second sentence indicates that verbal praise is endless, for speech follows the mind.
When the pivot of the mind is thus described, it is termed a "pivot. The general meaning is this: just as the heart of a door-pivot cannot be fully observed, [so too is this state].
It is exhausted; therefore, even when speaking to the ultimate limit, one cannot fully extol it. "Light" is also a form of praise, which here refers to its excellence.
My explanation based on these conditions cannot exhaust it; such words are spoken because it does not pertain to its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is beyond verbal expression.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "The Teaching Repository (Jiaofu) personally testifies," etc.: this follows from the preceding statement that one's own mind cannot fully express [the Dharma].

It refers to the scriptural treasury (jiaozang), wherein one personally testifies and offers praise. This brings rest to the explanation of the title. "Teaching" (jiao) may refer to this specific sutra or apply generally to other sutras as well;

"repository" (fu) is synonymous with "treasury" (zang). "Balance" (heng) refers to a scale for weighing lightness and heaviness, which precisely corresponds to this context: praising and distinguishing between superiority and inferiority. Therefore—
This preface and the verses of praise are called "Weighing" (*heng*). Because they explain the title, they are termed the "Title-Weighing.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase, "The six matters are cultivated together," the first two lines present the substance and the latter two lines point to the name.

The "six matters" are as stated in the sutra. As for the term "two causes," these refer to conditioned practice and vows; some say they refer to the middle and lower [capacities], and there are many such explanations. Taking contemplation as primary, one practices...

They serve as auxiliary causes. Now, it is feared that for the primary purpose of invoking [the result], six matters are required. As for what are called the "two," these are aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

These two kinds [of practice] act as the vanguard for the six matters of conduct. They guide and draw [the practitioner] so that the practice of the six matters does not stray toward other destinations.
Such aspiration and contemplation are termed "auxiliaries. The practice of the six matters constitutes the primary cause for invocation. Thus, by means of...
Regarding those that are named after their primary factor rather than their auxiliary factors: for example, the seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*).

For one who cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the preparatory concentration (*prayoga-samādhi*) is the primary essential, while mental attention serves as its auxiliary. Nevertheless, it is named after mental attention because, at the time of cultivation, the function of the latter is predominant.

Furthermore, for instance, although the essence of repentance (*paryavasthāna*) is remorse, it is called "shame and dread" (*hrī-apatrāpya*); likewise, [in other cases], it is named after that which diminishes power or increases benefit.

The essence that is capable of transformation is, strictly speaking, nothing but wisdom (*prajñā*). It is also said that through the cultivation of resolute belief (*adhimukti*), shame (*hrī*), and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), the two obstacles within the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) are diminished, and so forth;
yet in all such cases, their actual essence is never explicitly stated. These descriptions merely refer to what is proximate and predominant.

This is identical to how it is described here as "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*); the term "contemplation" encompasses six matters and is designated by way of its proximity. However, regarding practice...

It is correct that contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) serves as the auxiliary inducer; because one must not dare to depart from it during the time of practice, practice divorced from contemplation is termed "erroneous.
Therefore, its correct practice derives its name from its auxiliary nature. Question: Why is this not mentioned regarding those of middling or inferior capacity? Answer:
This explanation is given for the sake of the most prominent cases; in reality, all are termed "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).

Furthermore, the various practices listed among the middle and lower grades are also subsumed within these six matters, and are likewise termed contemplation. Question: What is the distinction between these three grades?

Moreover, this contradicts the direct commentary on the lower grades, as not all nine grades possess [these six matters] in their entirety. Answer: The lower commentary takes the primary [grade] as its main focus.

One cultivates these six practices, three karmas, and ten matters, which are divided into three grades. To achieve birth [in the Pure Land], it is necessary that all these practices mutually assist one another.
Furthermore, each of these three groups is subdivided into nine grades. How could the first and second grades within them lack mutual assistance and yet be shown to achieve birth in isolation?
Since the nature of their resultant retribution is not insignificant, there is no such thing as birth without cause; it is not the Way.

For the sake of principle, I shall briefly indicate one aspect: can those who possess or lack the precepts be born there? Therefore, the categories are distinguished according to the primary and secondary factors.
If their characteristics all involve these six matters, then the resulting fruits—whether internal or external—are none other than the karma of volition (*cetanā-karman*);
one cannot be born there if these practices are deficient. Within this meaning, one should engage in thorough investigation and deliberation, which will be further analyzed below.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the mother’s will was entwined with compassion for all wriggling creatures," she receives this name based on three causes, as explained in detail elsewhere.
"Entwined" (*cīna*) means to surround; it carries the sense of not being separated from [compassion]. "Wriggling creatures" refers to lowly insects.

By analogy with these, if she did not part from them even for such beings out of a compassionate heart, how much less so for others? Therefore, this is the ultimate compassion. "Embracing living beings" (*huái shēng*) is synonymous with "sentient beings" (*yǒuqíng*).
[This is] a name. Because it harbors consciousness (*vijñāna*) or afflictions (*kleśa*). [Commentary:
Regarding "Dàoyuán [attaining] the superior fruit," etc., the subsequent section explains the Bodhisattva. Two phrases distinguish their stage; two phrases designate their title.

Although they have in fact already attained Buddhahood, they manifest traces as causes and thus act as Bodhisattvas. As for the term "seeking enlightenment" (*qíjué*), it refers to obtaining the name of a Bodhisattva. It says...

Regarding "those whose destiny is birth," they receive the name *sattva*; this is based, for the time being, on their words of great vow (*mahāpraṇidhāna*). "The provisional is not real" concludes by demonstrating that it is a manifestation.

In the commentary: "Those called 'devas' (heavenly beings) possess radiant purity and sovereign spiritual function"—there are three meanings for the term "deva," which are easy to discern from the text. This...

[The text discusses] the various states of existence. Regarding the discernment of the realms (*dhātu*), when a Bodhisattva is born therein—whether in reference to arriving at that place or arriving among the assembly—it is termed "birth" (*upapatti*) in both cases.

[Commentary: As for the phrase "this is due to the celestial palaces of the Stage of Rebirth" (*ciuyou tiangong* etc. below, this section provides a general explanation of the intent behind establishing the title. First, it cites what is...
Contemplation. Next, the subject that contemplates is raised. The general intent is to lead people to contemplate and practice this, so that they may seek birth [there] and pay homage;
thus their vows will surely be fulfilled. As for the term "Successor" (Bupchu), this refers to the Bodhisattva mentioned in the title as Maitreya Bodhisattva.

As for the term "Celestial Palace," this refers to the Tuṣita Heaven mentioned in the title. When combined with the subsequent phrases regarding dwelling in peace and benefiting through transformation, one sees the aforementioned...

Regarding the meaning of the two characters "birth" (jō): this general intent states that it refers to a Bodhisattva in his final birth (ekajātipratibaddha) dwelling serenely within the Tuṣita Heaven palace, bringing benefit and transformation to all sentient beings.
This serves as the object of contemplation, enabling people to practice and pray for rebirth there without error.

Commentary: Regarding the statement "The *sūtra* (經) means 'to collect' (*saṃgraha*) and so forth," it enumerates four meanings. Having explained them in sequence, they are concluded by returning to two meanings.
To accord with principle (*li*) and accord with faculties (*gen*) is what is called a *sūtra*. "Collecting" refers to both the permanent and the Dharma, which is precisely the benefiting of beings;

this is "according with faculties. "Penetrating" (*guàn*) refers to the expression of the truth; this is "according with principle. As it is said in some places: "To collect is to gather these wondrous meanings; to penetrate is also to guide."
That "base" (yōng) is the opposite of this; there is no contradiction in interpreting it accordingly, as both can be applied to both the phenomenal (qíng) and the noumenal (lǐ).

Regarding the term "fence-cage" (fán lóng): it is said that "fén" (fán) means "cage. It is said that "fén" carries the meaning of being deep, dense, entangling, and obstructive. If the character for "affliction" (fán) is used instead, it refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) being like this.

Regarding "the hundred spirits" (bǎi líng): they are the divine and sagely. That which is unchanging is called "constant" (cháng). Regarding the "thousand petals" (qiān yè): they are the golden branches.
The "Jade Leaves" (Yù yè) refers to the Sovereign. All that is superior is raised as the victory, using this as a precedent for the rest.

The Commentary states: First, regarding the establishment of the provisional and the real by the Buddha—both the person of the Buddha and his teachings are termed "Buddha," such that nothing is left uncomprehended.
Question: Why is the character "accomplishment" (chéng) placed below? It is because the constant teachings of the Holy One speak of "attaining Buddhahood" (chéngfó).

Answer: Because these are two distinct gates, it is placed below. In the subsequent text, the provisional and real aspects of the Buddha are first distinguished, and only thereafter are the provisional and real aspects of "accomplishment" distinguished.
"Buddha" (fó) directly distinguishes the essence of the three bodies (trikāya), whereas "accomplishment" (chéng) distinguishes the process from cause to fruition. As for that Buddha...
The *Bhūmi-sūtra* first distinguishes its five dharmas and three bodies, and subsequently illustrates their partial realization across the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Therefore, it is appended there;

such is the arrangement of the text. If it were otherwise, the order of the characters would be inverted, serving no purpose other than to disrupt the composition and failing to accord with the flow of discourse.
Thus, from the perspective of meaning, fearing it might be confused with ordinary speech, I have set it aside as being of only a single significance.
Below, this will eventually cause readers to give rise to the seeds of divergent arguments; this shall be understood when we reach that section.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “*Quán* (expedient means) refers to responding to capacities and engaging with beings,” etc., the following explains the general meaning of *quán* and *shí* (reality). The matters and principles have not yet been fully exhausted.

That which is called "expedient" (upāya) accords with principle and phenomena; that which is called "real" (bhūta) accords with the ultimate truth. These two pairs are categorized separately and do not follow a fixed sequence.

To name something according to the capacities of sentient beings is "expedient"; to reveal the true reality is "real. According to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, to adapt to and engage with beings is "expedient"; to investigate the ultimate principle is "real."
Regarding this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, some current interpretations state that it corresponds to two other sūtras according to their sequence:

the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* investigates the principle according to the capacities of beings, while the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* accommodates sentient beings and reveals the truth. As for this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it contains two aspects of provisional means and one aspect of ultimate reality.

It is taught at random that there are three vehicles of ultimate attainment; however, because the two vehicles have not actually attained ultimate attainment, both the "ultimate" and the "non-ultimate" are designated as ultimate.
Since they do not exhaust phenomena and principle, they are provisional. Only when one thoroughly investigates principle is there the single vehicle of ultimate attainment.

Therefore, this is the ultimate reality; it is this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. As for the *Śrīmālā*, it teaches that four are real and one is provisional in order to lead those of the two vehicles back to the Mahāyāna by asserting that there is only the One Vehicle and no two vehicles.
Since there are actually three vehicles, its treatment of phenomena and principle is not exhaustive.
Therefore, this is the provisional (upāya). Since there are four [truths] that accord with reality, these four are the real.
When it is said here that the One Vehicle is provisional, this refers to the One Vehicle taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* designates as provisional;

it does not mean that the One Vehicle taught within the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* itself is also called provisional. In the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, True Suchness (*tathatā*) itself is termed the "One. This One Vehicle—

Because it exhaustively explains the principles regarding the production of the four vehicles and their subsumption within the four vehicles, it differs from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which teaches that there is only one vehicle and no second.

Therefore, the latter is provisional (*upāya*), whereas the teaching of the One Vehicle in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* is likewise real. This above has distinguished the provisional and the real based on the discourse.

To distinguish them based on the [Buddha] body: according to the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, these are manifestations adapted to the capacities of beings and are not accomplished through actual cultivation; thus they are termed [provisional].
That which constitutes skillful means (*upāya*) is called "expedient"; that which results from the thorough investigation of principles and cultivation is called "reality" (*bhūta*).

That which is for one's own enjoyment is called "reality," because it has not yet been taught that there is a self-nature body (*svabhāvakāya*). The intent of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* indicates that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* speaks of the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) separately in order to guide sentient beings;
this is also termed "expedient" because it does not revert to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), but is spoken of separately for the sake of guiding sentient beings. Furthermore—

To propose two Buddhas is not to exhaust the principle; it is termed provisional (*upāya*). To rely on what one has taught oneself, subsuming characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) back into nature (*dharmatā*), and establishing only the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), is termed real.
This is because a single person constitutes only one Buddha; thus, it exhausts the principle. Master Shan’s explanation says:
"Adapting to capacities is fundamentally for the purpose of engaging with beings; investigating the principle is precisely to reach the truth. Each has but a single meaning, as if..."
Regarding the headings and explanations, they do not originally consist of two pairs. Now, by forming two pairs and correlating them with the two sūtras, the sequence is also appropriate.
Although the names and meanings exist independently, they may be mutually attributed; following the meaning according to the intent involves no error.
Commentary: Regarding "the Buddha’s body speaks," this refers to what is taught through the commonality of teaching (*sāmānya-deśanā*); therefore, it does not refer to the formal doctrine (*śāsana*).

Furthermore, since the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) that are taught are also provisional (*upāya*), they are not called "real. Question: The *Lotus Sūtra* also teaches those of fixed lineage in the two vehicles. Since these exist as actualities and do not return to the Great Vehicle, how can one say there are three [vehicles]?
Is it not the case that these are real, and thus should not be called provisional? Answer: All [teachings] speak of the ultimate; yet in reality, they are not ultimate.
Therefore, this is also provisional (*upāya*). The Victorious One never taught it as ultimate; he merely said that such exists, and thus it is the real.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "This refers to the Half and Full Teachings of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*": this is based on the period before the two vehicles were integrated into the One Vehicle.

In that context, the Mahāyāna is called "Full" because it teaches the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), while the Two Vehicles are called "Half" because they teach only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). However, when [the teachings] are integrated, no such distinction is made.
The "half" and the "full" are both considered one.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "If the Tathāgata accords with their inclinations," this refers to the teaching in the *Lotus Sūtra* that [the three vehicles] are real;
however, this is taught as a skillful means (*upāya*). Skillful means is a provisional and expedient teaching, and thus it does not yet exhaust the ultimate principle.
The Commentary states, "That is to say, there are only... and so forth; this is the Commentary's explanation of the superior intention [of the sūtra].
The Commentary further states, "Regarding the Mahāyāna, Pratyekabuddhas," and so forth; below, it cites the four vehicles taught as real in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.

To say "those who have not heard" refers to those who lack the wisdom born of hearing. Because they do not possess the Three Vehicles, they are not vessels for the Dharma. To say "to bring them to maturity" means to cause them to mature;
this is conversion and deliverance. One converts and delivers them by means of their own goodness.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "If one sees us by means of form," this first verse dispels the view that the Buddha is to be seen as something like form.
"We" refers to the Buddha’s own nature, the Dharma-body; furthermore, it requires the gateway of subsuming appearances back into their fundamental nature, as well as the self-enjoyment [body].
Two phrases indicate the state of mind; one phrase dispels it. "Birth" refers to sentient beings.

To seek to see the Buddha by means of severing the path—just as one might seek to see form and so forth—is for such a being to be a sentient being who wanders upon the path of false severance. Therefore, they do not see him.
The final line serves as the conclusion. That treatise explains: "Just as that which should not be seen is invisible"—this refers to the three preceding lines of the verse.
"Just as that which should not be seen," and its invisibility, constitute the concluding final line. "Color-form" (*rūpa*) and so forth are termed "the objects" (*so*);
if one were to see them in such a manner, it would be improper.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "The wondrous body of that Tathāgata," etc., this is the second verse. As for the first three lines, because the Dharma-body is wondrously subtle, it should not be seen;
furthermore, it must be understood as being common to the self-enjoyment [body]. As for the final line, because coarse consciousness does not know it, it cannot be seen;
since consciousness manifests what is coarse, the words of the Guide refer to the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). This is the teaching of the Teacher of the Path.
It is the body (*kāya*). It is explained that it should not be seen. That treatise’s commentary states: "Just as it should not be seen, so too are the causes and conditions for its not being seen.
"Causes and conditions" here carries the sense of "the reason why. This corresponds to the final phrase [of the verse], because consciousness is coarse; the preceding phrase refers to the body.
This explains the first three lines. That [term] refers to the sublime essence (*sāra*). Since it is the *dharmakāya*, its essential nature (*svabhāva*) should not be seen.

Regarding the phrase "The commentary on that treatise says... and so forth: this verse does not explain the immediately preceding sutra; rather, it follows from the previous sutra’s definitive statement regarding the cessation of doubt.
Since it is not something seen and so forth, how can it be called a Buddha? How can there be any teaching [of it]? The sutra itself provides the definitive answer: "None."

There are fixed dharmas named *anuttara* and so forth; this is the explanation of those [terms]. Within this verse, there is also the self-enjoyment [body], which subsumes characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) back into their nature (*dharmatā*);

thus, it is collectively termed the *dharmakāya*. Therefore, [the other bodies] are merely the transformation and response [bodies], and not the true Buddha. Manifesting as a Buddha in accordance with the capacities [of beings] is called "response" (*nirmāṇa*).

Manifesting bodies according to various realms and classes is called "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*). Some say that the combined term [refers to] both the response and self-enjoyment [bodies], and is not [the *dharmakāya*].

The "True Buddha" does not refer to the literal meaning of the text. One should rather say that it speaks of the Dharma-body as the locus of reality (*bhūtārtha*), which subsumes the self-enjoyment [body].

To speak of the self-enjoyment body is termed the locus of expedient means; this is said in reference to distinguishing it separately from the fundamental [Dharma-body]. The first phrase dispels the body, and the second phrase dispels the teaching;
these are also manifestations, for they are not the actual teaching. Furthermore, there may be doubt, thinking: "Since it was said that the response and transformation [bodies] are not..."

Regarding the "preacher of the Dharma": it is not that one who responds through transformation fails to preach the Dharma at all. Therefore, the subsequent sutra states: "The Dharma preached by the Tathāgata is not grasped and cannot be spoken;
it is neither dharma nor non-dharma. Now, this verse says: "In preaching the Dharma, there is no dualistic grasping," for duality is itself the [conceptualized] dharma.
The following line further explains this: the speaker has no reality, and that which is spoken is beyond words. Thus, it was said above.
The commentary states: "Not one who preaches the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "taking the Dharmakāya as the reality," etc.: in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the marks are subsumed back into their essential nature; this refers to his self-enjoyment [body].

It is also called the *dharmakāya*. The meaning is identical to that in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*. The subsequent statement that the two bodies are merely the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*, and lack the *svasaṃbhogakāya*, refers to this.

Regarding the commentary’s remark, “this takes the *saṃbhogakāya* as the reality,” it means that while the *Lotus Sūtra* has not yet spoken of the *dharmakāya* of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-dharmakāya*), it does speak of the *svasaṃbhogakāya*.
That which is used is called "real," because it is accomplished through actual cultivation. That which is called "transformation" refers to the maturation of others;
it is not accomplished through actual cultivation, as it arises through manifest transformation.
Commentary: Regarding the two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): as for the first set of four, it does not distinguish according to the specific type [of being];

rather, it refers to that which possesses the marks of a Buddha and designates it as "Buddha," and only then does it differentiate the four propositions therein. In this context, the minor transformation body lacks the sense of receiving the bliss of the Dharma, and thus cannot be called "retribution" (*vipāka*).
As for the second set of four, since it differentiates according to the specific type and designates it as "Buddha," that which possesses the marks of a Buddha is then termed [the Buddha].

Because it is a retribution [body], even a minor emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) enters the first four phrases. Alternatively, the first four phrases—referring to the enjoyment of the bliss of the Dharma that resembles the self-enjoyment [body]—are alone designated as "retribution" (*vipāka*);
this does not extend to minor emanations. Within the category of mere emanations, those that are shadow-like abridgments or conform to the various classes [of beings] are excluded.

The second set of four phrases refers only to the Buddha’s marks, which are then designated as "retribution"; these do extend to minor emanations. As for the self-enjoyment [body] and... [the text continues].

The nature-body (*svābhāvika-kāya*) is analogically categorized with the enjoyment-body for others (*para-sambhogakāya*). There are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) respectively; in both lower cases, they are identical, while only the two instances of the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) differ.
Furthermore, in the *Fayuan zhang*, the correspondence between the "response" (*nairmāṇika*) and the "transformation" (*nirmita*) is treated as four permutations.

That [text] does not designate the enjoyment-body for others as a "transformation," which contradicts this [view]. Each follows its own specific meaning, and thus there is no fault. That [text] refers to...
That which manifests as the body of a Buddha is called "response" (nirmāṇa); that which manifests as the bodies of the five destinies is called "transformation" (nirmita).
Therefore, the sixfold response-body of the sixteen-foot form is also a transformation, because it first manifests as a human and subsequently attains Buddhahood.

Now, in this context, we refer to what arises through manifest transformation as "transformation"; thus, even the Body of Enjoyment for Others can be termed a "transformation," and there is no contradiction.

Commentary: Regarding the first point, "The Dharma-body is called 'conformity with reality' (*yathābhūta*)," etc., a question is raised: For one who must subsume characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) back into their nature (*dharmatā*), the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) is already included within the section on reality.

To then speak below of the "remaining two"—the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*)—is not contradictory, because the reward body encompasses both the self-reward and [other-reward], as they correspond to each other.
