Furthermore, this does not conflict with the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which speaks of the self-enjoyment body.

Because the use of the body is termed provisional (*upāya*), the answer is as follows: that which is subsumed within the nature (*dharmatā*) is also established as real-provisional when contrasted with the distinct [manifestations].

Since a single person accomplishes only a single Buddha, it is termed "real. Apart from the *dharmakāya*, the description of the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) is a provisional trace, as it remains hidden within the *dharmakāya*.
Even if one speaks of two distinct [bodies], this is because a single person accomplishes two Buddhas; thus, it is likewise [provisional].

This is a provisional trace (*upāya-pada*). Question: If that is so, when the three bodies (*trikāya*) are distinguished, is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) also provisional? Why is the Dharma-body exclusively termed "real" (*tattva*)? Answer:

When the end is distinguished from within the source, the source is hidden as one; when the end is subsumed back into the source, there is no remainder as one. Question: [What is the meaning of this?]
Although the preceding objection has been refuted, how is the subsequent objection to be addressed? Since it is directly contradictory to the *Vajraśekhara*, the answer is as follows:

Just as the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* points to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as being provisional (*upāya*), this case is likewise so. This refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* in relation to the *Vajraśekhara*;

specifically, the *Svasaṃbhogakāya* (Self-Enjoyment Body) is designated as "provisional" because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* had not yet manifested the *Svabhāvikakāya* (Nature Body), whereas the *Vajraśekhara* does encompass it.

Since they have not been explained separately, some have said that that which possesses arising and ceasing is called "provisional" (upāya), while that which is without arising and ceasing is called "real" (tattva).
Therefore, they claim that self-enjoyment [wisdom] is termed provisional. Now, I say this is not so.

If only the nature and characteristics were considered real and provisional, I fear this would not capture the essential purport of "real and provisional" in this context. Thus, in this heading, it simply says "conforming to reality."
In the commentary, it simply states that "the essence of all dharmas is real," and there is no mention of "only" or "arising and ceasing.

Regarding the phrase "provisional traces of phenomenal characteristics," this refers to teaching that phenomenal characteristics themselves are the Buddha; this is a provisional expedient. It is taught provisionally for those who have not yet realized the fundamental dharma-nature.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "second, the Dharma-body and so forth," this is categorized as two bodies and differs from what was previously stated.

Furthermore, these are also established as real through the completion of actual practice. Question: Since the *Lotus Sūtra* has not yet spoken of the Dharma-body, how can the two bodies herein be considered real?

Answer: It also incorporates other teachings and can further clarify them; moreover, it reveals that the *dharmakāya* is the reality, as when it says, "The characteristics of the world are eternally abiding," and so forth.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "Only Buddhas are equal to Buddhas": the two bodies are listed above, while the ten meanings are established below to conclude by returning to the general name.
Two phrases form one sentence, and one phrase forms another sentence; subsequently, the five meanings each consist of only a single phrase.
Since all these two bodies and ten meanings are identical, they are therefore collectively termed the "True Body" (*dharmakāya*). As for the statement "the basis of this body," it is for...

Regarding the phrase "the basis of transformation": it means that they are equally free from differentiation, unlike the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* [heaven], where there are distinct levels of superiority and inferiority.

Regarding the phrase "merit and wisdom, etc.": this refers to the self-enjoyment [body] (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), which is identical to the *dharmakāya*. The *dharmakāya* does not speak; or, if one uses the term "merit," it may be applied to the *dharmakāya*.

Regarding the phrase "cannot be described by color, form, etc.": this is because, in terms of being devoid of shape and magnitude, the two bodies (the *svasaṃbhogakāya* and the *dharmakāya*) are identical. There is no [difference].

Regarding the statement that the head, feet, and other distinct parts have no spatial limits or dimensions: the previous mention of "boundlessness" referred to the functions of individual dharmas, whereas this refers to the body as a whole.
Alternatively, the former refers to being inexhaustible at the furthest reaches, while this refers to pervading the ten directions.

As for the phrase "arising and ceasing," the character "without" (無) carries over to the following; this refers to coarse characteristics, because both the [heavenly] others and the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* heavens manifest coarse forms of birth and death.
Commentary: Regarding "the Body of Enjoyment for Others" and so forth, each should be understood as the inverse of what was previously explained.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "Thus the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* says," etc., the preceding section distinguishes the provisional and the real aspects of the Buddha, while the following section distinguishes the accomplishment of the provisional and the real;

this general category is termed "the Buddha’s Accomplishment of the Provisional and Real. This does not conform to the common expression "attaining Buddhahood" (*chengfo*), the intent of which lies herein. If one were to conform [to that common usage]...

It is commonly said that there must be two distinct ways of investigation; otherwise, what benefit would there be in overturning them? It is not for the sake of sentence fluency or ease of pronunciation.
Because the character *chéng* (成) stands above [the other characters], it is easier to pronounce. Thus, this intention is intended to provide a point for generating divergent arguments.
Within both "Buddha" (佛) and "accomplished" (成), there are each provisional and ultimate aspects. To speak of "Buddha" alone is to discuss "Buddha" directly, without further deliberation.

Regarding the cultivation of causes: if that [attainment] is accomplished, there must be one who accomplishes it through the cultivation of causes; this constitutes the textual passage. It places the result first and the cause afterward.

Furthermore, within this discussion of accomplishment, its result is also connected; although only "accomplishment" is explicitly stated, the intended meaning is the accomplishment of Buddhahood (*buddhatva*).

This refers to the textual passage concerning the body of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi-kāya*), which serves as a conclusion and verification for what precedes it and gives rise to what follows. Below these two points, its accomplishment is analyzed.

There are no such meanings [in those other texts]. One should contemplate their subtle functions. From here below, the characteristics of that which is accomplished through cultivation (*bhāvanā-samudāgata*) are explained;
therefore, it is not permissible to say that the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) cannot be said to be "accomplished," for its essence first arises, and thus it is called "accomplished.

Generally, the term "accomplishment" (*samudāgama*) applies to both [the innate and the cultivated]. Question: This sutra is one fascicle, while the treatise (*śāstra*) has seven fascicles; yet it speaks only of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and its...
Regarding the four wisdoms, there is no textual passage concerning these two bodies—the provisional and the real. How, then, can they prove what precedes? How can they give rise to what follows?
Answer: This is not a citation of a text; rather, it is a statement based on the underlying meaning. That [text] explains five dharmas, which directly proves the two realities.

Furthermore, within the context of the Wisdom of Equality and the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks, it speaks of the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Thus, these two are the provisional. This proves what precedes. As for that...

Later in the sutra, it further states that upon attaining the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and partially realizes the single flavor (*ekarasa*);

this is precisely what constitutes "ability to accomplish," which occurs subsequent to this [present life]. In the seventh fascicle of that treatise (*śāstra*), there is also mention of "actual form" (*bhūtavarṇa*) and "transformed form" (*nirmāṇavarṇa*).

Since transformation is provisional (*upāya*), and since transformation corresponds to the body, it is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) as a reflection. Otherwise, why would he cite this here? This is what was stated at the beginning.

The reason for this is that it must necessarily connect with what precedes it; the following section cites this very point and explains it. Thus, one knows that this text further initiates the subsequent major divisions of the treatise.
These constitute the seventh topic of that treatise: the five dharmas and the three bodies, which correspond to the Buddha himself.

What the Sūtra describes as the ten stages (bhūmis) is precisely the realization of the Perfected Reality (*pariniṣpanna*). What the Treatise describes as "manifestation" is the sequential responding to the capacities of sentient beings. This is...
[The Master] Chengquan requests that you examine this closely.

In the commentary: "However, regarding these 'actual bodies' and so forth," within the section on establishing [the doctrine], the actual comes first and the provisional follows. Within this discussion of the actual, one first presents the essence of what is established;
this consists of four phrases. This applies to both bodies, and it is connected to what follows below in the section on establishment.

The text concerning "power" (*quan*) is the direct opposite of [the text concerning] "substance" (*zheng*). This can be seen by examining them side-by-side. Although it is raised as being "upon the body," it essentially has no fixed location; it is contrasted with "power" to form a pair.

As for its self-nature body (*svabhāvakāya*), although its essence is non-dual with the dharma-nature land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*), it is categorized under the Buddha-dharma because its characteristics and nature are distinct;
thus, it is also termed "body and land. Since the fundamental true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) has no fixed location, it is established as...
The body and the land likewise have no boundaries; because their meaning pervades the entire substance, they are called "pervading the dharma-realm.

Alternatively, this dharma-realm refers to empty space, as can be known from its own nature; since it is neither exclusively east nor exclusively west, it is called "without direction or location. This is not the case for the provisional body.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "The Dharma-body is originally present," etc., the following provides a detailed explanation. Since the two bodies are distinct, their two meanings differ;
in each case, they are first indicated and then established through analysis. These two phrases [state that] the Dharma-body is originally present and, furthermore, is common to both.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "all those who, through forgetfulness, concealment, and so forth," this is raised first as an instance of non-attainment, prior to the formal resolution to attain enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), because there is no fixed limit [to such states] before that point;

thus, they remain entirely unaccomplished. As for the term "store" (*garbha*), its meaning is "to contain. Although they are not yet called Buddhas, they contain the meaning of Buddhahood and are therefore termed a "store.
"Tathāgatagarbha" (the Tathāgata-store) is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "by means of associating with virtuous friends" and so forth, this explains the attainment of the stage below, yet it remains connected to that which is about to be cultivated as the cause.
Some sources describe afflictions (*kleśa*) as the "store" (*kośa*), but that is not employed here; for the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* distinguishes two stages based solely upon True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "one may simply say it is realized," etc., the fear is that an outsider might suspect: "If the Dharma-body has existed from the beginning, how can it only be accomplished upon reaching the fruit?
The two phrases of the commentary answer this by clarifying that the name "accomplishment" refers to realization; it does not mean accomplishment as a process of production.

Therefore, there is no contradiction. The outsider further suspects: "If all untainted dharmas are realized, and this is already the case in the ten stages (*bhūmi*), why is it that only the Buddha-fruit is called [the state of] 'realization'?"
Regarding the Dharma-body: furthermore, although one may have realized it, if the realization is not yet perfected, it is not called the Dharma-body.
Within the ten stages (bhūmis), the noble path is not yet complete, as all various merits have not been fully attained.
Commentary: Regarding the passage beginning with "The self-enjoyment body, etc.," this four-line text sets forth the preceding *dharmakāya* by way of contrast, as the two meanings differ:

the former is not produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-saṃskṛta*) but is fundamental, whereas the latter consists of distinct individuals rather than being a single unity. Having thus set forth the distinction, one may then proceed to analyze the sequence of its cultivation and realization.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and so forth," there are three subsequent stages distinguished by whether they are unaccomplished, about to be accomplished, or already accomplished.
Accordingly, we first distinguish the unaccomplished stage, which is that of one who has not yet generated the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "by drawing near to virtuous friends" and so forth, from the point when a Bodhisattva sits upon the seat of enlightenment until the actual attainment of perfect awakening, all of these constitute the stage of "about to achieve.
From the moment the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) is generated until before Buddhahood is attained, there is a period with a definite limit;

all of these belong to the stage of being about to achieve perfect awakening. It is not merely that which is immediately adjacent [to Buddhahood] that is called "about to achieve. These three practices of proximity constitute...
This first line provides a general summary. To explain it according to its meaning, the following citations serve as proof. From the *Vajra* [Sūtra] onwards, all [stages] cause the seeds to increase;

since they have not yet attained Buddhahood, they are all termed "treasuries" (*kośa*). In all ten stages, the Buddha serves as one's virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), because one listens to the Buddha’s Dharma.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the ālayavijñāna, etc.," the ālayavijñāna is ultimately unreal and can be severed; therefore, it is termed "empty.
This [consciousness] is able to contain and store the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*). These untainted seeds, named after their fruit, are called the Tathāgata.
Thus, the emptiness of the Tathāgata’s store is the Tathāgatagarbha. Furthermore, in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, it is also taught by means of afflictions...
It can ultimately be severed. That which conceals the *dharmakāya* is called the "empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
Although the interpretation is similar to what was explained previously, it is not what is intended here. Here, the *ālayavijñāna* is termed "store" (*garbha*);
this does not include the afflictions (*kleśa*), and thus does not contradict the intent of the scriptural passages.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "endowed with perfuming," the *Amogha-kośa* (Not-empty Treasury) takes the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) as its essence.

In terms of the relative relationship between cause and fruit, the cause serves as the treasury for the fruit; this is largely the same as the *Tathatā within bondage* discussed previously. Therefore, the names of the two sutras are distinguished below.
However, this receives the name "Treasury" only from the point when the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) has been generated onward; hence it says, "endowed with perfuming."
Regarding the seeds of cultivation: those who possess the sevenfold supreme perfuming, or those who are fully endowed with the Mahāyāna mind, all receive this name.

They proceed directly to the Vajra stage. This differs from what was stated previously, where it was said that from the point of first generating the mind until the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one is not yet named the Dharmakāya, but is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Question: Is it partially named the Dharmakāya? Answer: It is partially named the Dharmakāya. The *Fayuan* (Garden of the Dharma) also states that [the state of] the ten stages is [partially] the Dharmakāya.

Because the three bodies (trikāya) are established therein, it may also be partially designated by the name "enveloped" (saṃvṛta). Previously, it was taught only for ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) and termed an "ālaya.
Furthermore, this is because the seeds of outflows (āsrava-bīja) are identical [in both cases].

Commentary: Regarding "generating the mind, practicing," and so forth, the preceding section provided a general explanation; from here below, the discussion is based on the stages (*bhūmi*). I shall first indicate the detailed exposition and subsequently provide a brief analysis.
As in the *Xin jing shu* (Commentary on the Heart Sutra), which cites the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* to explain this extensively, I cannot cite it at length here.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "in the stage prior to the grounds" (*bhūmi-pūrvaka-avasthā*) and so forth: below, the text properly relies upon the stages. Within the stage prior to the grounds, it first distinguishes correct cultivation.
What follows from this constitutes its karmic fruition (*puṣpa-vipāka*): possessing a body and a land, as can be understood from the text.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "from the first bhūmi onwards," within the stages of the bhūmis, the provisional rewards (*puṣpavipāka*) are also distinguished.

First and last, the six heavens of Jambudvīpa and the false views of the first dhyāna are established; these, together with the latter three, are termed the ten. The Bodhisattvas of the ten bhūmis may be understood accordingly.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "yet not yet [attained] the untainted (*anāsrava*) and so forth," there are two sentences with two meanings.

It is not entirely untainted; even if it were untainted, it would still not be complete. This distinguishes it from the stage of Buddhahood. These two sentences explain the reason for this distinction:

since the true body (*dharmakāya*) is precisely the eighth transformation, if that [stage] is not yet untainted, this [stage] should likewise be so. Furthermore, its fifth and eighth [consciousnesses] have not yet become untainted. Therefore.

It is not yet complete. Question: Of the one hundred and forty kinds of causes, how many have already been attained? Answer: Only these marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) are attained during the causal stage;
the remainder are attained only at the stage of Buddhahood.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "giving rise to the Enjoyment for Others" (*parasaṃbhoga*) and so forth, the following section distinguishes the lands (*kṣetra*). When both compassion (*karuṇā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) increase, both give rise to the retribution for others.

As for those in whom compassion increases, they manifest lands according to the various types of beings (*yathā-jāti*), as stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* regarding the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmi*), where it speaks of the thousand-petaled lotus and so forth.

Following the previous principle, this reveals what follows; it clarifies that there are large and small [lands], or it reveals that the bodies themselves possess large and small dimensions, rather than serving as proof for the manifestation according to the types of beings.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "after the Vajra Path," etc.: within the Vajra-mind, there are no further "flower-rewards" (intermediate rewards);

there is only the "actual reward" (ultimate fruition) that extends back to what preceded it. This section below also concerns the stage of imminent accomplishment. Although it speaks of provisionally attaining the marks and signs of the outflows-free state, this clarifies that these are attained before long;
it does not manifest a sequence of stages already fully realized. This continues until the citation of the *Yogācārabhūmi* below.
Having concluded [the previous section], the subsequent passage states: "In the stage of the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*), the body still possesses outflows (*āsrava*)," and so forth.
This refers to the stage of completion. Such instances where the text concerning the completed state cites prior causes to connect the preceding with the subsequent are extremely numerous.

In this case, however, it is the reverse: the posterior is used to clarify the anterior. This is as in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā*: "Because one abandons the two types of heavy obstructions (*dausthulya*), one realizes the transformation..."
[This] is based on [the fact that it] still distinguishes the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “However, as for the various bodhisattvas,” etc.: the above section generally distinguished the cultivation and the accomplishment; from here below, there is a specific distinction of the stage of transformation (*pariṇāmiki-bhūmi*).
First, the explanation of what is attained and abandoned is in terms of the stages; subsequently, the explanation of the dwelling place is in terms of the heavens. First...

Within the stage of attaining the [Buddha] position, two categories may be known: those in whom wisdom predominates and those in whom compassion predominates. Regarding the phrase "as if entering the meditative absorption of cessation" (*nirodhasamāpatti*):

in the state of entering the absorption of cessation, one necessarily subdues the afflictions (*kleśa*) and does not undergo further *pariccheda-vedanīya* (segmented) rebirth; instead, one requires the support of *pariṇāmi-vedanīya* (transformative) rebirth. Therefore, the absorption of cessation is shown to clarify this transformative rebirth.

Commentary: Regarding "the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and so forth," the following section distinguishes [the process of] further provisioning (*punar-upasaṃhāra*). Since one does not abandon [the seeds] while in the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), they must be provisioned once again. Commentary:

Regarding "until the stage of the Vajra-turning (*vajravartana*) where they are finally exhausted," this is precisely what distinguishes abandonment. If "turning" (*vartana*) is taken in the sense of arising, then the actual abandonment is termed "abandonment.
Alternatively, this term "turning" refers to the turning-abandonment (*vartana-prahāṇa*); like the abandonment at the Vajra [stage], it can be understood as having already been abandoned.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "by this, the seventh stage, etc.," the following section distinguishes the dwelling places. It clarifies only the increase of compassion (*karuṇā*), as it follows the pattern of the increase of wisdom (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, this refers only to those who proceed directly (*ekāyana*); for those of gradual awakening (*anupūrva-abhisambodhi*), their dwelling places are not fixed.
It specifies only the Bṛhatphala heaven, because its location is most excellent; it excludes the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, as these are the abodes of the śrāvakas.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "relying on this lower stage," etc., the former portion distinguishes birth, while the latter portion distinguishes reliance.
Furthermore, there is both initial reliance and subsequent reliance. That which is called "lower" is relative to Maheśvara, or else relative to the Śuddhāvāsa [Heaven].
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "about to reach the Vajra [stage]," etc., this below distinguishes the subsequent destination where one attains Buddhahood;
it does not distinguish the act of relinquishing, as that has already been distinguished previously. Furthermore, all cited proofs concern only the location and never mention relinquishing.
Since one has already reached that place prior to the Vajra stage, it is termed "about to."

Commentary: Regarding "transcending the three realms," this is explained according to the auxiliary causes of the untainted (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, it is stated either in terms of the most excellent [attainment] or in terms of following from the Buddha.

Commentary: Regarding "benefits such as the present retribution," this does not concern distant cultivation; rather, it refers to attaining Buddhahood through the indestructible diamond-like state (*vajrāmṛta*).
It is for the sake of the present-life retribution (*dr̥ṣṭadharmavedanīya*). Although one has abandoned the outflows (*āsrava*), it is not called "death.

The body born from the station of wisdom (*jñānasthāna*) of Maheśvara—since its karma must have been created prior to the stages of the *bhūmi*—and considering this celestial body, since it has already undergone birth and death, it constitutes a future-life retribution (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*);

its fruit is likewise superior. Furthermore, in terms of attaining Buddhahood, it is termed "benefit" (*hitakara*). Question: As in the stages of equipment (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*), does one enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) without dying? No, one enters.

Regarding those who go there after undergoing transformation (*pariṇāma*), they should also experience retribution in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*). Answer: Those who go directly must be born in the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) heaven before they can rely upon transformation;
therefore, there is no retribution in the present life. This explanation is not correct. This would apply only to those of gradual awakening (*anupūrva-abhisamaya*). One should state this:

since this karma is the karma that brings about the general [rebirth], it necessarily lacks retribution in the present life. Question: Should there not be retribution in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*)?

Answer: This is not defined in relation to the four types of karma. Rather, it is designated as "present retribution" (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya) when the fruit is experienced immediately by the very body that performed the action.

That which is separated by a birth is all termed "subsequent retribution" (upapadyavedanīya); thus, even karma that is to be experienced in the next life is called subsequent retribution. This interpretation is correct.
As for the term "place of wisdom" (jñānasthāna), it is uniquely so named because it is the place where Buddhahood is attained; it is the locus of wisdom.
"Abode. Maheśvara is precisely the abode of wisdom (*jñāna*). His tenth stage involves relinquishing this abode to be born in the abode of wisdom.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the stage of the Vajra-mind" and so forth, this will be distinguished below as already established. Although the "Vajra" is mentioned, it is merely intended to provide a comparative distinction with the Buddha-stage.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "these cultivated [bodies], such as the *nirmāṇakāya*," etc.: from here below, the main text concludes by returning to the provisional and the real (*śakyasiddha*).

The two bodies—the *dharmakāya* and *sambhogakāya*—are called "real" because they accord with the realm of true wisdom. "As" (*ru*) has the meaning of "conforming"; it signifies the profound union of wisdom and its object. Alternatively, it means "resembling.
Since both are devoid of the dualistic grasping of subject and object, they are termed the "two aspects of suchness" (*liang ru*).

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "those two provisional bodies" and so forth, the following section establishes the nature of their being provisional. It first juxtaposes the other two bodies—the Nirmāṇakāya and the Saṃbhogakāya—against the preceding Real Body (Dharmakāya).

While the former has no fixed location, these [two] do. Although their distinctions are set forth, they manifest according to what is appropriate; the underlying intent concerns their spatial location.
Alternatively, this may be a separate textual passage that supplements the preceding two bodies. If one were to discard these provisional bodies, there would be no concluding text below. This...
This is the introductory text; since the meaning is fully evident, it is said to be "according to what is appropriate.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "As for the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) and so forth," this section below provides the proof. "As for" (*zhi*) means "for now" or "temporarily"; "as" (*ru*) is a demonstrative pronoun.

It refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Body) as "only" (*zhi*), indicating that the Transformation Body has not yet been discussed. Furthermore, regarding the Transformation and Enjoyment bodies, it first clarifies the bodies and their lands; there are further [details] to follow.

The characteristics [of these lands] will be discussed later. Furthermore, because they are all relatively concise, they are termed "only" (kevala). The first three lines and the remainder constitute their transformation-retribution [lands].
By citing the Bodhisattvas who perceive the transformation as the principle, it reveals the magnitude of the other [Buddha’s] retribution bodies and lands.

The phrase "one hundred Buddhas" refers to the great transformation; one great transformation Buddha reigns over one great trichiliocosm. Within one great trichiliocosm, there are ten billion small [trichiliocosms].

Transformation. This section, following the principle above, is the commentary on the text. What is called "ten billion" refers to the minor transformations (*kṣudra-nirmāṇa*). This points back to what was previously mentioned, though its major transformation (*mahā-nirmāṇa*) had not yet been stated.
By clarifying that there are ten billion minor transformations, it is shown that the preceding one Buddha constitutes a single major transformation. This is the major transformation.
There are ten billion small transformation bodies, and for every hundred of these, there is one great transformation body;
thus, these together constitute a single seat of retribution for transformation, corresponding to the first stage (bhūmi).
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "this refers to the Enjoyment Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya*) and so forth," the following section is the text that distinguishes the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Although the term "two emanations" has already appeared previously, this section now specifically and fully distinguishes them—both collectively and individually—in order to clarify the Enjoyment Body.

This is the general introductory text. Within it, first the realm (*kṣetra*) is presented, followed by the vision (*darśana*). Regarding the vision, the mention of "this former [stage]" refers to its preparatory application (*prayoga*); the hundred [qualities] are omitted for brevity.
Regarding the phrase "hundreds of millions of provisions" (*koṭi-sambhāra*): next, there are the two lines below, or perhaps the two lines above, which together form the heading for what follows.

Second, the specific classification of the transformation [bodies]. Because of this, the commentary below explains that sentient beings have superior or inferior capacities; hence it says "gradations. The Buddha perceives their great or small [capacities] based on this.
Although this refers to the body, the text connects with the preceding meaning, and the intent also clarifies the land (*kṣetra*). Or, it may refer to that which is manifested for them.

Below is the measurement of the body. The Master of the Commentary (Sū-zhǔ) often arranges his prose in reverse order; here, he places the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sāmbhogikakāya* within the land, and the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sāmbhogikakāya* within the body—this judgment is most excellent.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "what is seen in the first bhūmi" and so forth, this distinguishes the Buddha based on his seat. Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "the bodhisattva of the first bhūmi" and so forth, the body of the bodhisattva is equal in measure to that of the Buddha; this is called "correspondence.

Alternatively, manifesting as teacher and disciple with [the Buddha] being half their size is also called "correspondence. Otherwise, it would not be the case that they are not different from those prior to the bhūmis. Furthermore—
There are those who cannot equal even half [of the Buddha’s qualities], and thus they are not commensurate; hence it is said that they are "many.
Regarding the phrase "from the first bhūmi onwards" and so forth: an external opponent asks, "At what stage prior to the bhūmis are the bodies not equal to the Buddha?
Or are there some that cannot be commensurate with the Buddha, being only half as great? Upon entering the bhūmis, they become determined and become commensurate with the Buddha. Or...

Regarding the phrase "those whose names and characteristics correspond to half [of them]," the commentary explains that because they have already attained the concentration of untainted merit (*anāsrava-guṇa*),

they differ from those prior to the stages who have not yet attained the untainted; there is a considerable difference in their rank, such that some may be extremely inferior and unable to correspond,
or may not even equal half.

Commentary: Regarding the "divided" (*prādeśika*) and "transformative" (*pariṇāmika*) [births], an external questioner further asks: "If Bodhisattvas also possess divided and transformative births, why can they all equal or approximate half of a Buddha?
As for their 'divided' births, they ought to be small. The intent of the commentary’s response is as follows:

Although they differ in coarseness and subtlety, their magnitude is the same. This is because even that which is initially small is nourished by outflow-free merit (*anāsrava*). Here, the term "large" refers to...
That which is equal to half of a Buddha is called "great," because it is compared to the physical stature of beings in the human realm today.
Since the Buddha’s body is extremely large, that which is equal to half of it is "great" by virtue of its resources.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "at the rank of the ten kings" and so forth, this second interpretation is likewise not fixed; it is the same as [the case] prior to the stages (bhūmi).
As for the statement "either receiving or not receiving," since there is internal reception within, the body's dimensions are identical to those of the class of beings they follow.

This means that even here, some are unable to equal half the size of the Buddha’s body, because the Buddha is of the ultimate magnitude. What is seen at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) is the Enjoyment Body for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*).
The Buddha’s body is sixty million *koṭi-nayuta* *yojanas* in height; such is the text. Question:

Since the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of the preceding moment is only half as great, how is it that the subsequent moment increases by so much? Answer: This is because one has newly acquired the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) provisions;
this has already been explained previously.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "correct wisdom realizes suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth," this clarifies the wisdom that takes [suchness] as its object.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the ten hundred gates of illumination (*vidyāmukha*) and so forth," this is based on what is taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 47, which states that in each and every moment (*kṣaṇa*).
1. One realizes one hundred samādhis. 2. With the purified divine eye, one sees one hundred buddha-fields. 3. One sees one hundred Tathāgatas and shakes one hundred worlds;
one’s body is also able to travel there, emitting great radiance and so forth. 4. One transforms into one hundred types of beings, allowing others everywhere to see them.
5. One brings to maturity one hundred types of sentient beings who are to be converted. 6. If one wishes to prolong one's life, one attains the ability to remain in the world for one hundred kalpas.
Seventh, he perceives events throughout a hundred kalpas of the past and future. Eighth, through his wisdom-vision, he is able to enter the "Gate of Illumination of a Hundred Dharmas.

Ninth, he is able to manifest a hundred of his own bodies. Tenth, he is able to manifest a retinue of a hundred bodhisattvas. These first three samādhis exert their influence downward into the subsequent stages.
Commentary: If one attains a thousand dharma-gates upon reaching the second stage (*bhūmi*), it is double that of the previous [first stage].
Question: Are all subsequent stages ten times greater than the preceding ones? Answer: According to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, they are not merely ten times greater.

In the latter ten fascicles of that twelve-fascicle work, the ten stages are established separately, with one fascicle dedicated to each stage. Within the first stage, one realizes a hundred [qualities] in a single thought-moment.

Samādhi. Such as these: two thousand in the second stage, one hundred thousand in the third stage, ten million (*koṭi*) in the fourth stage, ten billion (*nayuta*) in the fifth stage, one hundred billion in the sixth stage, one hundred thousand billion *nayutas* in the seventh stage, a number equal to the atoms in a three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system in the eighth stage, a number equal to the atoms in a hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-fields in the ninth stage, and ten [times that] in the tenth stage.
It may be said that [the merit] is equal to the number of atoms in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds.

According to this explanation, the third, fourth, and sixth stages are each a hundredfold; the fifth stage is a thousandfold; and the seventh stage is a nayutafold—wherein a nayuta consists of billions upon billions.
As for the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages, compared to the preceding stages, no such multiplication is perceived; they are not like those [lower stages].
This will be explained in detail later. If each stage were ten times the previous, the total number would be extremely small;
by the tenth stage, one would only reach ten trillion (where the "billion" above is calculated as ten million, which is a *koṭi*). A *koṭi* multiplied by a *koṭi* is a *nayuta*.
In the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), ten thousand is often taken as a "billion" and termed a *lakṣa*.
Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the Buddha’s seat and his body are proportionate," their measurements are not identical; rather, [the seat] is mostly half the size of the body.
The Bodhisattva’s body measurement is likewise half that of the Buddha, which is why it is said they are "also thus. Alternatively, the body need not necessarily be exactly half the size of the seat;

it simply must be smaller than the seat, being proportionate as appropriate. It is difficult for the Bodhisattva’s body to be exactly half that of the Buddha’s, yet their mutual proportionality is likewise so. This is not because...
"Half and half" means "likewise. Regarding the phrase "like emanated disciples and so forth," the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha also possesses them.

There are actual bodhisattvas and emanated bodhisattvas; these emanated bodhisattvas correspond equally with the [actual] half. Although this arises from karma, it is certain that they are manifested by the Buddha's mind.
Otherwise, why would it be necessary to cite such an example?
Commentary: Regarding the passage beginning with "I, the present Vairocana," the following serves as a scriptural citation.

Furthermore, in reverse order, this second stage consists of two phrases concerning the retribution of others, two phrases concerning great transformation, and four phrases concerning minor transformation.
The Commentary states: "Also like Amitābha Buddha and others" refers back to the first bhūmi.
The Commentary states: "The *Lotus Sūtra* also says... and so forth; these two passages below do not specify which bhūmi [is meant], and thus they are general.
Since Śāriputra is also a transformed bodhisattva, it is not seen that he was manifested as a bodhisattva of any specific bhūmi; therefore, this is also general. Or perhaps...

Because it is for the most part pleasing to those who prioritize the initial teaching, it was cited at the beginning. Furthermore, these two passages serve as evidence that the Enjoyment Body for Others (parasaṃbhogakāya) manifests according to the specific types of beings;

thus, its dimensions, size, and location are not fixed. As for Mañjuśrī, he is present in the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and therefore he is one who manifests according to the specific type [of being].

Question: Why is there no separate explanation of the Emanation Body (nirmāṇakāya) from the second bhūmi downward? Answer: Although the number [of such emanations] gradually increases, [the text does not provide a separate explanation].
Its measure is equal to the first [assembly], and therefore it is not treated separately. However, among them, those who have the cause for it are sparse;
thus, regarding the *Avataṃsaka* assembly and so forth, one merely takes up what is not seen to clarify that it is his retribution. It is not necessary to cite those who do see it as proof.
Those who cite those who see it are merely Mañjuśrī, and he is not a Buddha. Question: Mañjuśrī is at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"In which stage is this located? Answer: "The manifest does not exclude it; furthermore, it is provisionally established as a proof by following the categories [of the stages].
It is not a proof for any specific stage’s category. Commentary:

Regarding "that which is observed by the subsequently attained wisdom" and so forth, this accords with the provisional and ultimate meanings of the *Vajraśekhara*. Based on the distinct subsequently attained wisdom, both...

The aspects of the movement follow one another, entering into the realization of reality (*tattvadarśana*). Question: What is the difference between this and what was previously stated regarding "correct wisdom realizing suchness" (*samyagjñāna-tathatā-sākṣātkāra*)?

Are they not redundant? Answer: The former is based on whether [reality] is seen or not seen; this is based on seeing the provisional (*prajñapti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*). Question: Does the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) not see the self-enjoyment [body]?

Answer: This is merely a case of being exclusively provisional and exclusively subsequently attained; fundamentally, it only takes the ultimate as its object. When the principle is fully exhausted, [it is subsequently attained].

One attains the supernormal power of taking both the provisional and the ultimate as objects. Thus, they are practiced in tandem; however, they are explained separately according to their specific meanings.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "if the tenth stage, etc.": the preceding section has distinguished the first two stages, while the following section directly transcends them to distinguish the ten stages.
This may be examined in detail in the text.

Commentary: Regarding these various lands and so forth, the following section distinguishes their characteristics. First, the *vipāka-bhūmi* (retribution land); second, the *nirmāṇa-bhūmi* (transformation land). Within the retribution land, there are three sections.

Here, the discussion of those born in evil destinies such as women and so forth—the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to those without sense organs (*anindriya*) and the like, which constitute the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*).

In the subsequent citation of scriptural evidence, first the absence of female organs and the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) is proven, followed by the proof regarding animals; the remaining cases are to be understood by analogy. Within this, the great...
[The] *Yi* [commentary] states: "It is essential that there be no characteristics such as those of a child in the womb. The *Shu* [commentary] states:
"'The Drum-Sound King Sūtra and others' refers to the following reconciliation of contradictions. An external opponent asks: "If there are no women, how can there be parents?
The phrase "If there are none" [in the text] serves as the reconciliation; although the words "parents" appear here, they are used solely for the sake of this reconciliation.

Regarding the passage on "coming from among women": this is not intended to definitively establish the absence of parents; therefore, the following section briefly further establishes that there are no parents.
Regarding the phrase "There is an interpretation, etc.": the previous interpretation held that Amitābha’s land is exclusively a *vipākabhūmi* (retribution land).

This master, however, interprets that Amitābha Buddha encompasses both the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and the *vipākakāya* (retribution body). Although there are women in Amitābha’s land, they nonetheless do not exist within the retribution land itself.

This is not a contradiction. However, while Amitābha’s land possesses both the reward body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the transformation body (*nairmāṇikakāya*), the text below cites Śākyamuni as also having both the reward and transformation bodies, just like Amitābha.
Nevertheless, within the reward land, there are no transformed parents.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "However, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says... and so forth, this actually supports the previous interpretation. Within the reward land (*saṃbhogakāya-kṣetra*), there are manifested parents;

it is not necessary to claim that Amitābha encompasses both the reward and the manifested lands. Alternatively, there may be an interpretation that asserts Amitābha encompasses both his reward and manifested aspects.
This further proves that within the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward land) there are transformed parents; thus, these two meanings coincide.

Since Amitābha universally manifests through transformation, both Śākyamuni and Amitābha—whether in their *saṃbhogakāya* or *nirmāṇakāya* forms—possess transformed parents. The intent here is that Māyā is the mother.
Furthermore, it is said that those who are "contained" must be transformed bodhisattvas who have gathered there; this refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation) land.
Regarding the passage from the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* cited below, this is intended to distinguish the characteristics of those who previously resided in the heavens.
Therefore, the commentary cites the concluding portion of the sutra, which states: "It does not say where they originally dwelt," and so forth. Within this sutra, there is only this statement...
The commentary states: "Attaining Buddhahood while remaining in their seats. This applies to both Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
As for the question "Why is this so?", the following section explains the reason why they do not manifest in the heavens; this location is for the sake of bodhisattvas.
One attains Buddhahood right here; therefore, he first came from the Tuṣita Heaven to serve as a Mahāsattva, so that there would be no need for him to undergo long periods of longing beforehand.
Below this, Maitreya is cited in contrast: this is because those of lesser capacity must be made to rejoice for a long time.
Only then can he be seen; therefore, he first dwells in the heavens and subsequently descends to be born.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "his other enjoyments" and so forth: the preceding sutra of the *Hīnayāna* (lower vehicle) establishes that he has no parents. The three phrases cite and indicate this:

he sits directly upon the throne without mentioning any other matters, thereby clarifying that he has no parents. Having raised this point, the two subsequent phrases provide the corresponding conclusion.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "for instance, the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and so forth," this refers to the superior recompense for those above and the inferior transformation for those below. Briefly, four characteristics are distinguished.
In the text, the capacities of sentient beings and their respective lands are first cited as the reason why the land of recompense is not uniform; thus, the word "for instance" (*qiè*) is used.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "when about to become a Buddha," this distinguishes the arising of contentment and the non-arising [of rebirth] in other heavens, as can be understood from the text.
As for the term "about" (*jiāng*), it refers to the period prior to his presence within the assembly of Śākyamuni; that which is prior is not yet "about.
Furthermore, while residing in Tuṣita, he may also be called "about," in contrast to the actual accomplishment [of Buddhahood].
Commentary: "As for Śākyamuni and the others" refers to the signs of his descent [into the world]. To distinguish his descent, he first indicates his presence in heaven.

The word "only" (zhǐ) is used here to point specifically to these two [Śākyamuni and Maitreya], as no others are being considered; this is why the term "three periods" (sānjiè) is not used later, where it would otherwise be redundant.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "attaining Buddhahood at the three periods," this refers to the aspect of subduing Māra. The mention of the Bodhi tree and so forth is stated for the sake of contextual convenience, or perhaps as a complementary contrast.

As for the seat being exclusively vajra while the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha possesses the seven jewels, the reason they differ in their subduing of Māra is that the sequence differs, as explained elsewhere.
Alternatively, regarding the four or two [types of] Māra armies, they are not identical; refer to the text for details.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the Vajrāsana path and so forth," this refers to the characteristics of attaining enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*). It is because [the Buddha] manifests such characteristics as well;

this is not a statement of ultimate reality, for the textual context is interrupted. Question: Although the principle may be so, how is it seen from the text that these are manifested characteristics rather than actual realization?
Answer: It says, "for the sake of benefiting sentient beings," which clarifies that these are manifested characteristics.

Commentary: Regarding the *Sūtra on the Past Lives* (*Pūrva-yoga-sūtra*) and so forth, these were previously discussed in a general manner; since we have now entered this specific sūtra and it speaks of "its accomplishment," they do not constitute the main text.
Herein, first, the Dharma-body and the two types of retribution are excluded.

This exclusion of the principle of the Dharma-body refers only to that which can be realized, namely the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Following this, under the phrase "also not," the two types of retribution are specifically excluded. That is to say—
[The text] below refutes [the objection] and returns to the original point.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Although it mentions the transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*) and so forth,” this anticipates an external question:

"How can one speak of the provisional (*upāya*) without speaking of the real (*bhūta*), and yet still achieve real benefit? The commentary below addresses this by showing that the provisional reveals the real because their characteristics are similar. As it says:
Because one perceives the moon in the sky through the moon in the water. [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "the self-enjoyment body and so forth," the following serves as an explanation. First, the provisional and the real are discussed; thus, their characteristics are taken as the underlying principle.
By means of the real, the provisional is manifested; since the provisional resembles the real and the provisional is not separate from the real, it can be made manifest.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "Although... and so forth, the following section addresses and resolves potential objections. An external questioner further asks:

"If the provisional is used to manifest the real, and since provisional bodies are many while the real body is one, the two preceding phrases should be negated. The meaning does not deviate from what was stated before; now, these points are restated in order to set forth the subsequent text.
The general meaning may be understood.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Like the moon emerging from the edge of the clouds,” the first four lines serve as a metaphor for the three preceding verses.

Regarding the phrase "below the manifestation of the vessel," this is a metaphor for the inferiority of those who perceive it. In general, there are two intended meanings. The first meaning is that the provisional is manifested through the real, like the moon manifesting its reflection;

by observing the reflection, one knows the moon, and thus the semblance of True Suchness can be manifested as a reflection. The second meaning is a metaphor for the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*):
although there may be hundreds, thousands, or billions of them, the actual body is but one. This can be understood by reversing the sequence accordingly.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the two bodies of the true and the provisional," this is the application of the analogy. It applies [the analogy] to the convergence of the provisional and the real.
Therefore, the section beginning with "one should know" should not be connected to this; rather, it concludes that this [preceding part] is solely the provisional.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "Thus the *Pātra-sūtra* says," etc., these two passages together serve as proof that Maitreya is both provisional and ultimate.
This first indicates the passage where it is not yet known [that he is a Buddha], followed by the passage proving that Mañjuśrī will soon attain Buddhahood;

therefore, the present Maitreya is a manifestation of a Buddha, for he is already a Buddha, whereas Mañjuśrī is not yet known [to be so]. If he were a real bodhisattva, such would be his appearance and measure, [as is the case with] Mañjuśrī.
[The interlocutor] says: "He must know. [The questioner] asks: "Mañjuśrī is already a Buddha of the Constant Joy (Sadāpramudita) realm, and Maitreya is also a Buddha;
Mañjuśrī should therefore know this. Why do you say he does not know? [The respondent] answers: "This refers to one who *will* become a Buddha, not one who has *already* become so.

The intent of citing this case here is to clarify that those who are adjacent to attaining Buddhahood are what is being discussed. That which is 'not known' here must already be a Buddha. Since he is already a Buddha, it is now possible to see him."
Therefore, this is an emanation (*nirmāṇa*). Some say that this proof establishes Mañjuśrī as an emanation; however, this is not what is intended here.

Alternatively, it may be because they do not understand the principle of the text: Mañjuśrī is an emanation, and Maitreya is likewise. This is because an emanation is contrasted with an emanation, and a reality with a reality.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "all bodhisattvas and so forth," within the context of establishing the provisional and the ultimate, this refers to the establishment of the number of births; it distinguishes the number of births required for the attainment of Buddhahood.

Commentary: "Bound by one more birth" means that because there is still one remaining birth as a binding condition, they will attain Buddhahood immediately upon leaving [this life]. This refers to Maitreya.
During his time in the assembly of Śākyamuni, there was yet one more cycle of birth and death. When he descended from heaven, that body did not perish until he attained Buddhahood;

therefore, it is called "the final. Furthermore, with this very same body, when he was about to attain Buddhahood, he sat upon the seat of a Bodhisattva, which is called "sitting at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
The place where one attains the Way is named the "site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Commentary: Regarding the statement, "Because Buddhahood arises from causes, all three are exhausted," this distinguishes between what is set aside and what is established. When discussing the Buddha-body, distant [causes] are not considered;
therefore, they no longer exist.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "only the transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇakāya*) and so forth," this text connects with what follows.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "as in the seventh stage and so forth," this is not the same as what was previously stated—that one further coming and going constitutes "one birth.
Here, it merely refers to three stages within a single *pariṇāmikakāya* (transformation body). Alternatively, what is being discussed here refers exclusively to this single body.

The single body of one more birth-and-death that was previously separated [from the state of non-retrogression]—namely, this very last body of one more birth-and-death—is what immediately undergoes transformation (pariṇāma).
This preceding body is what is called "the body bound by one birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

For example, in the case of the seventh stage, while remaining among humans, there is still one more birth before one is born in the fourth dhyāna and undergoes transformation; this preceding human body receives the name "one birth. Its...
The "final body" (*paścima-deha*) refers only to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), in terms of the transformation of support (*pariṇāma-vaśitā*).
In reality, however, the final momentary body of the seventh stage that undergoes transformation is also termed "final."
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "bound by one birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*), this refers to the second fundamental existence (*mūlabhava*) of this body; it is the body bound by this single lifetime.
However, there is no textual passage stating where that [existence] is located.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "if one speaks of those among the devas," this clarifies that it does not refer to these cases.

Commentary: "Thus there are three" means there are three intervening stages. Taking the previous human body as the starting point and looking toward the subsequent attainment of Buddhahood, excluding the body of the Buddha, there are three minor births.
The body of the Buddha cannot serve as an intervening link; therefore, it is not mentioned.
Commentary: Regarding the first point, "the removal of calamities for beings" and so forth: within this passage, sentient beings are presented first, followed by non-sentient things.

Among sentient beings, three types—animals, humans, and devas—are presented; furthermore, among humans, three types—the physician, the artisan, and the king—are presented. These can be easily seen by examining the text.

Commentary: Regarding the second point, "beings born according to their kind" (*yathā-jāti-ja*), there are also three parts within it: first, the designation of those who are born; second, the identification of the purpose; and third, a further indication. Commentary:
Regarding the fourth, "superior birth" (*abhyudaya-ja*), since the previous second section only mentioned animals and so forth, this is opened up separately and combined with them.
All of these may be considered as "conforming births" (*anupapatti-jāti*).

The commentary states that those who possess the latter four types of birth are shown to be identical to the gods because their physical form and color are superior, because they are heavenly kings, and because they are also most excellent;

it is only not the case that they are born to eliminate calamities and afflictions. Regarding the fifth [category] mentioned previously, this refers for the time being to the final body; in principle, however—

The celestial body (*devakāya*) is also excluded because it is subsequently designated as one of the "great births" (*mahājāti*). The second explanation below holds that only the middle three [of the six perfections] are complete, and thus does not rely on the category of great births;
therefore, the fifth is excluded, as it has not yet attained the state of supreme excellence in comparison to the attainment of Buddhahood.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "if one is born in this continent, etc.," the former [passage] explained the bodies of the devas, while this explains the lower bodies; it refers specifically to those that are most excellent. Question:
Why would there not be births such as those of Mahāsthāmaprāpta in the lower realms? Answer: This merely follows the previous increase [in merit]; it does not preclude the existence of others.
Commentary: "A countenance of outstanding distinction" refers to an extraordinary appearance that rises up prominently; it is most remarkable.
*Jin* (矜), pronounced with the second tone for both characters *ling* (凌) and *ju* (巨), means to cherish or take pride in.

Commentary: "This is precisely the child's aspiration" refers to what follows in the second explanation, which accords with his innate disposition and conduct; or, as in the second explanation below, this also applies generally. Commentary:

"The uncle gives birth to the disciple of the master" means that because both master and disciple benefit one another, the task is accomplished; thus the uncle acts as the master and the outsider becomes the disciple.

The Commentary states: "As for why there are four questions, it is because the first question—'My teacher Pārali possesses how many marks?'—is followed by three subsequent questions, all of which concern the marks possessed by Pārali."

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "The Buddha, taking the opportunity, manifested transformations," this refers generally to sixteen transformations. As it says below regarding their rising from their seats: "They all rose from their seats.
Then, regarding the teaching of the skillful means, it says they returned to their places. Next, it says: "The other fifteen persons attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Again, as it says below:

"They all became Arhats (the fruit of the worthy one), with the sole exception of Maitreya, who was not included among them. This means that Maitreya desired to seek Buddhahood and thus did not join that group.
This refers to realizing the fruit of a śrāvaka’s state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). It does not mean one who is not included among those of the renunciant class.
Regarding the commentary on "spinning with one's own hands": the character *jì* (績) is pronounced *dí* (狄) in the even tone; it means to weave or to ply thread.
Commentary: "No one dared to take it" means that [the man] knew himself to be unworthy of the task.

Commentary: "When Maitreya was about to pierce the pearls," etc., refers to how, having been rebuked by his wife, he felt intense remorse and distress; thus, he caused her to realize they shared the same karmic fruit.
Furthermore, he wished to cause that wife as well to have faith and compliance.
Commentary: "The Buddha [spoke] because of Aniruddha" refers to Āniruddha.

Because the Buddha [recalled] his own offerings to pratyekabuddhas during previous kalpas and the merit and benefits thereby obtained, he then spoke of the future fruit of Maitreya. At that time, Maitreya made a vow, saying:
"From now until I become that Buddha, I shall serve as a pearl-stringer for him."

Commentary: Regarding "the site of the tranquil extinction (*śānti-maṇḍala*)," *śānti* (tranquil extinction) is the name for the principle (*tattva*), and the place where that principle is realized is called the *maṇḍala* (site).
Commentary: Regarding the *Maitrīcitta-samādhi-sūtra*, among the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), it is named after the most prominent one, following the conventional order.
In reality, however, it explains all four kinds. Each of these four has three grades with respect to sentient beings. A brief diagram is provided as follows: [Diagram omitted]
Commentary: "Unable to be subdued" means that because they could not cause the Buddha to submit, they themselves were subdued. Commentary:
Regarding "if there are those of the animal class, etc.," the first verse-line is the refuge in the Buddha; three lines are the refuge in the Dharma; two lines are the refuge in the Saṃgha;
and the final three lines are the concluding exhortation.

Commentary: Regarding "circumambulating the sage seven times," it is often performed seven times because [the practitioner] follows the Seven Buddhas, because of the seven aspects of body and speech, and because of the flowers of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment.
Commentary: Regarding "the sage addressed him" and so forth: Question—The sage is supremely compassionate; how does he praise and accept [the request]? Answer—He addresses the sage...

At that time, he merely spoke of "making an offering" and did not say "throwing [the body] into the fire. As for the *Ṛṣyaśṛṅga* and others, this is also termed "giving up the body"; thus, the ṛṣi praised him.
Next, when it says "giving up the body," it still does not mention death; therefore, the ṛṣi did not stop him. Alternatively, the subsequent words may not be addressed to the ṛṣi.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "compassion cannot respond," this means one is unable to speak; thus, one writes to decline the request. Furthermore, the desire to inquire about the *piṭaka* and the scriptures is also expressed in writing. Commentary:
Regarding the two lines "I would rather kill myself or gouge out my own eyes," the first line expresses his own feelings, while the second verse relies upon the Buddha. The first verse is as follows:
Relying on the precepts, the subsequent verse describes the benefits and disadvantages.
The commentary states: "The earth shakes in six ways" refers to two types: first, in terms of the sixty thousand [yojanas];

second, in terms of the six phenomena—namely, shaking, surging, trembling, striking, roaring, and bursting. These latter five types are all derived from the initial term "shaking. Furthermore, because they are all states of instability, they are collectively termed [earthquakes].
[The word] "movement" [is explained in the] Commentary: "Those who have attained the Way of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa" does not mean that they are the thousand Buddhas themselves;
rather, it refers to those sentient beings who have heard the Dharma and thereby attained the Way of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "this explains the initial time," etc., the following section provides a clarification. As for the name "Maitreya" (慈), it was not derived from the mother's name;
rather, it was established by physiognomists based on the child himself. It simply refers to the child, though it arises from seeing that the mother’s compassion is directed toward the son.

Knowing the child’s nature to be compassionate, the name "Compassionate One" (慈) was established; it is not a name derived from the mother. Therefore, the later explanation returns to the original Sanskrit, where there is no such character as "na" (那). The preceding...
Because she was ordained as a *bhikṣuṇī* from among the nuns, she is called "the first. This is because there are two sections concerning her in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*;

this refers to the first instance. As for what is called "the one who approached," this is stated in the sūtra in contrast to the *ṛṣi*. According to the tradition of this title, they refer to one and the same person.

Commentary: If one relies on this "nature" (xing), it refers to the nature of conduct; this distinguishes it from what is named after one's mother. At that time, one should have been named according to the nature of one's conduct;
yet now, this [surname] is instead derived from that [maternal name] and called a "clan" (xing).
Commentary: Regarding the statement that "there are many lineages among the Brahmins," this is a general rebuttal. An opponent asks: "Previously it was said that he was born into a Brahmin family;
why then is it now said that his clan is Maitreya? The intent of this answer is as follows:
That [Brahmin] is a general surname, for within the Brahmin caste there are many specific lineages. Tradition holds that there are eighteen clans among the Brahmins. This is...
First. Regarding the commentary’s mention of "Maitreya and others," this master’s intention is to say that these were names in ancient times and are not surnames even now;
they are simply names. As for "Ajita," this is translated as "Invincible."

Commentary: Gautama is his clan name (*gotra*). Question: What is the distinction between a "clan" (*xing*) and a "lineage" (*wang*)? Answer: A distant ancestral lineage may be designated as a "lineage";
that which has not undergone any change is simply a "clan."

Commentary: Regarding the statement that "there are many kinds of kalpas," these include the small, medium, and great [kalpas], as well as the periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness, and those caused by fire, water, wind, and so forth;
all of these are explained within the verses of the Chapter on Kalpas.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "contemplating Bhaiṣajyarāja and others," the three thousand Buddhas appeared over the course of three kalpas; this is first explained in general terms.
Furthermore, the causes from their past lives are first recounted, while the details concerning their initial emergence are subsequently distinguished separately.
Commentary: Regarding the third, Vipaśyin Buddha—according to these seven [kalpas], the first Buddha among them does not belong to the *Vyūha-kalpa* (Adornment Kalpa).
Vipaśyin Buddha belongs to the first kalpa of the *Lakṣaṇavyūha-kalpa* (Kalpa of Auspicious Signs). Śikhin and Viśvabhū both belong to the thirtieth kalpa of the same *Lakṣaṇavyūha-kalpa*.
Because they are separated by such a vast distance, and since Viśvabhū Buddha belongs to the *Vyūha-kalpa*, [Vipaśyin] is therefore [not of that same period].
This is not that kalpa. It is the ninety-first kalpa, which is this Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Kalpa).

Beyond Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa Buddha—passing by these six Buddhas in total—and including Śākyamuni as the one encountered, there are seven; thus, it is commonly said that there are seven Buddhas.
This refers to Śākyamuni; within the kalpa of his marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), the subject and object are shared. These aforementioned kalpas refer to the fire calamity (*tejaḥ-saṃvartanī*).
According to this adornment, compared to the Bhadrakalpa, they are separated by sixty kalpas, or by sixty [kalpas] of increase or decrease.
Adorning the Bhadrakalpa. As the great kalpas are adjacent to one another, the subsequent interpretation is considered superior.

Regarding the phrase "the three thousand Buddhas and so forth" in the commentary: the question is asked, "For what reason do the three thousand [Buddhas] simultaneously resolve their minds toward enlightenment and attain Buddhahood, yet not within a single kalpa?
This commentary answers it. The general meaning is as follows: although their initial resolution of the mind is identical, there are three grades in their cultivation.
Regarding the third point: each of them individually practiced superior deeds and together realized the fruit; thus, they [attained it] over the course of three *kalpas*. Question:

Since the three thousand [worlds] should each have their own bodies and lands, why does this text speak of "practicing together" and "realizing together"? Answer: This statement refers to being together within a single *kalpa*;
it does not mean that they exist simultaneously at one and the same moment. If it were otherwise, then Śākyamuni, Maitreya, and Lohitākṣa...

Regarding the Buddhas, how can it be said that their bodies and lands are merged? There are still those who claim that the merging of nine hundred and ninety-four Buddha-bodies and lands is incorrect.

Commentary: Regarding the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* and other texts, the preceding section generally distinguishes the three *kalpas*, while the following section specifically distinguishes the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Aeon).
Here, the *Vimalakīrti* is cited to generally distinguish the aforementioned ancestors. King Ratnacchattra made offerings to Bhaiṣajyarāja for five *kalpas*.
Among this king’s thousand sons, there was one named Prince Candracchattra; he, too, made offerings to Bhaiṣajyarāja for five *kalpas*. Their characteristics are as follows.
Next, regarding "attaining Buddhahood":
The commentary states, "The *Sūtra on the Five Turbidities* says, etc. This refers to the appearance of Buddhas within the Bhadrakalpa, which is divided into three periods of time.
There were four Buddhas in the past, including Śākyamuni; however, only three are listed below because the present [discussion] still pertains to the Dharma of this Śākyamuni. [End of] Sūtra.
Regarding the Buddha’s body, Śākyamuni has passed away; the intent of the commentary concerns the Dharma, while the text pertains to the present.
Furthermore, because it is intended to be contrasted with Maitreya, they differ. Among the three [periods], the first two differ in name and also in the number of kalpas;
these are discrepancies in translation that cannot be reconciled. The verse in the chapter on kalpas states: "Sixty thousand, forty thousand, and twenty thousand [years]—the Kṛta age."
The one called Anagha-Kāśyapa is here translated as Kanakavatsa, which refers to Krakucchanda.
The one called Kanakamuni is Kanakamuni.

Commentary: Regarding the passage beginning with "The Bhadrakalpika-sūtra says," etc., the following section describes Śākyamuni. It does not continue from the preceding sūtra but instead separately describes the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Aeon), with the intention of bringing him into alignment with Maitreya;
thus, these two Buddhas of the present are presented in contrast.

This mention of "human lifespan" refers to the period during the final dharma (mappō) of Kāśyapa Buddha, which coincides with the appearance of Śākyamuni Buddha when the human lifespan was one hundred years; both belong to the ninth kalpa. This is the first [point].
[Regarding] "increase and decrease":
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states that the life-span in Tuṣita Heaven and so forth differs from what is described below; this is an error of the translator.
[Regarding] "the human life-span turns, etc.": Below this, one intends to distinguish the appearance of Maitreya in the world; this connects to the *Bhadra-kalpika-sūtra* to distinguish the kalpas.
This citation does not serve to clarify the meaning of the *kalpa*. When it speaks of the time of Śākyamuni Buddha’s True Dharma (*saddharma*), human lifespan was not decreasing;
this is an error by the translator. As for the phrase "thirty or twenty years," the character "three" (*san*) is used three times [as a multiplier]; otherwise, there would be a contradiction.
"Shū" (疎) means "sparse" or "rare.

Regarding the statement that "the son's age is double that of the father," according to the *Zuǎn* (纂), this refers to being born at ten years of age and reaching fifteen; exceeding half [of the father's age] constitutes "doubling.

"Shū" (疏). Regarding the passage beginning with "increasing by sixty thousand," etc., this section above generally distinguishes between increase and decrease, while the following section below specifically distinguishes the appearance of Buddhas. This is so.
The claim that Maitreya appears during the aeon of increase (*utsarpiṇī*) must be erroneous, because King Rāghava lived during the aeon of increase.
The following citation from the treatise refutes this, for it is necessarily the aeon of decrease (*avasarpinī*), not the aeon of increase.

Commentary: Regarding the statement, "He first appeared when the lifespan was eighty-four thousand years at the beginning of the period of decrease": Question: Since it is stated immediately below that he appeared when the lifespan was eighty thousand years, why is it said here that it was eighty-four thousand?
Answer: At the very limit of the initial decrease, the figure of eighty-four thousand was established; thus, it is called "the beginning of the decrease.
This does not mean that he remained [in the world] for exactly eighty-four thousand years, but rather that from that point, the lifespan decreased down to eighty thousand years.
At that time, it was still called the "initial" [eonic period], as it belonged to the first of the three divisions.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that human life expectancy was eighty thousand years when [the Buddha] first descended to be born: this is connected to the preceding hundred-year mark and seems to fall within a single period of decrease (*apacaya*).

However, the mention of "a hundred years" refers to the ninth period of decrease; after the decrease has finished and the increase (*vivṛddhi*) occurs, following the tenth period of decrease, it reaches eighty thousand years once more. Mī... [text ends]
He emerged from his seclusion. It was not during a single *kalpa* of decrease. Question: How long is the lifespan of such a Rākṣasa?
Will he be able to meet Maitreya Buddha? Answer: Over four hundred thousand years. Question: Eighty-four thousand [years] is the maximum; how can there be so much longevity? Answer:
Generally speaking, it corresponds to that time. As for eighty-four thousand, this is the limit of merit; beyond this, it transcends [calculation].
There is no error here. This is because figures such as Pengzu and Laozi lived five times longer than that.

Regarding the phrase "erecting one great stūpa," this refers to the time [of Śākyamuni]; the *Sutra on the Descent into Birth* states there will be eighty-four thousand, which refers to a later period.
Alternatively, this statement may be interpreted as meaning that the extinction of Śākyamuni’s Dharma will likewise occur in that manner.

Commentary: Regarding the passage beginning with "The *Bhadrapāla-kalpa-sūtra* says," etc., the preceding section distinguished the two Buddhas who appear in relation to the intermediate period, while the following section distinguishes all the Buddhas of the future thereafter.

This too first provides a general distinction: this sutra cites the third Buddha, Kāśyapa, through to the exclusion of the last one, totaling nine hundred and ninety-nine Buddhas who share a single kalpa;
