According to the sūtra, it mentions only the characters of the *brahmī* script, which belongs to the Western regions (India).

As for why the sub-commentary (*shu*) subsequently cites the characters of this land (China), it is to demonstrate that at that time, if people of this land had also been there, the meanings of the characters of this land would likewise have appeared clearly within the light. "Huan" (煥) means manifest; "lan" (爛) means...
This means "clear.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase, "merely beholding the text," etc., it is intended to address the potential objection: "How can one perceive its meaning within the light?

This [phrase] serves as a response to that, because the characters are manifest and their meaning is fully understood; thus, it is also called "radiant" (*bingran*). It is not merely that the eyes behold...

This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "immediately upon [hearing] the Sūtra, he arose," etc.: because he did not delay even for a moment, it is called "seeking" (*vitarka*). This is not the "seeking" of *vitarka-vicāra*.
Regarding the phrase "although his body entered nirvāṇa," etc.: because it causes people to make offerings, it is a benefit of the Dharma (*dharma-lābha*). *Śarīra* (relics) is called "Dharma. Or...

This is the representation (*vijñapti*). It is called "Dharma" because it represents the Dharma. While the previous [stūpas] represented meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), this represents the benefit of the Dharma (*dharmārtha*).

Question: Since the characters were manifested previously, why did they not represent the Dharma? This [previous case] merely involved the construction of a stūpa; how is it related to the Dharma? Answer:

Furthermore, it is said to be for the sake of the meaning (*artha*). This represents that which is to be explained (*vācya*), causing people to make offerings. This is the unsurpassed benefit. Because, in the future world, there will be only the Dharma remaining.
Therefore, although his wisdom and concentration were actual, they were not seen by the world.

[The] Commentary [states]: "Within that platform" means that this seat is situated upon the platform. Within the hall, upon the platform, there is the seat of one who possesses this fearless sitting (*abhaya-āsana*).
Question: According to this, it should be that there is a platform within the hall, and the seat is placed upon that platform. Why is this so?

Regarding the scriptural passage concerning the mani-palace within the pavilion of the seven treasures, the *Daichō* (Great Commentary) states: "The 'pavilion' (*t'ai*) refers to the foundation and steps.

How then is it explained in the sub-commentary (*sho*) that "within that pavilion, the position of the Dharma King is supreme and he has attained fearlessness"? It should now be understood as follows:
According to this sequence, it should be said: "Upon the lion throne within the seven-jeweled terrace atop the maṇi-palace.
This scripture follows the Western tradition of placing the agent before the object; hence it is so.

It is not possible for the terrace to be placed inside the palace, therefore it should be said "upon the steps"; and because the throne is placed within that terrace, there is further a lotus upon the throne.
Regarding the lotus: the sub-commentary (*śāstra*) explains it itself. Upon the lion throne, there is yet another lotus, along with four tiers of palaces; these constitute his seat.
However, that lotus appears within the section on the "characteristics of arising" in the latter part [of the text]. Here, in the former part, the lotus has been omitted.
Furthermore, in the preceding section, it instead speaks of "apparitional birth" (*upapāduka*); this is all intended to lead the reader through the textual passages. Now, I shall explain it again.
It is said: The previous mention of "place of birth" (*janmasthāna*) refers to both "birth" (*janman*) and "place" (*sthāna*). In this term, the word for "flower" (*padma*) is omitted.

This present mention of "birth-characteristic" (*janmalakṣaṇa*) likewise refers to both "birth" and "characteristic. The "birth" mentioned previously refers to the latter four modes of birth; the "birth" mentioned here refers to the initial arising, as can be understood from the preceding text.
The first phrase of this sutra, "upon a lotus flower," distinguishes this initial arising. Otherwise, how could it be possible [to be born] upon this?
Furthermore, why is the lotus not mentioned? It is because the lotus is essential for establishing the initial arising;
since the seat and so forth are not raised [as primary], the flower is not mentioned in the preceding section. Regarding these "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa), there are two kinds:
first, the four modes of deportment; second, physical appearance. This may be understood from the text.
Commentary: Regarding "sitting in the full lotus posture" (*paryaṅka-bandha*): "binding" (*bandha*) means to coil and bind; placing one foot upon the opposite thigh is called "lotus" (*paryaṅka*).
According to this commentary, the full lotus posture is divided into two types: the Subduing (*vajraparyaṅka*) and the Auspicious (*bhadraparyaṅka*). There are not three types.

Alternatively, if there are three types, they consist of the single term "subduing," the single term "auspicious," and that which is neither bound nor crossed, but simply has the feet placed directly against one another.

Regarding the left and right: within the manner of binding [the hands], there are also variations of left and right, upper and lower, which correspond to the *paryaṅka* (full lotus) posture for subduing, as well as the *paryaṅka* posture for auspiciousness (*bhadrapīṭha*). Here, we take the full-lotus auspicious posture.
Because the right hand is used first, when the right is on top, it is for the purpose of performing [an action]; when the right is underneath, it is for the purpose of commanding.
Non-action is the cessation of evil; this is subjugation, therefore the left hand presses down upon the right. The performance of all virtues brings about auspiciousness;
this is the creation of fortune, therefore the right hand presses down upon the left. Since this [rite] is intended to cause rebirth in Tuṣita, one should therefore adopt the auspicious [position].
Commentary: "Virtue so high as to be peerless" is a general indication that the physical stature of this [being] far surpasses that of the celestial hosts;
it signifies that his virtue is so exceedingly high that there is nothing with which it can be compared. Sixteen *yojanas* amount in total to two hundred and fifty-six *li*.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the stature of those celestial hosts is calculated to be one *li* and forty-five paces. Question: How is it that he descends below?

Śākyamuni and others exceed only half [of the limit]. The answer is: because human vessels are small, they attain their place by exceeding only half; because celestial beings have much pride, they must exceed to the very limit before being pressed down.
Regarding the commentary on "able to transcend the six realms" and so forth: this is a specific indication. Question: Why not directly indicate sixteen matters for each single case?
Thus, two [categories] below represent sixteen *ya*. The answer is: this is also a single matter intended to manifest that which transcends both the mundane and the supramundane.

The followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) remain within the inclusion of the six realms of existence (*ṣaḍgati*); as their characteristics do not transcend the class of the six destinies, they are not included [in the higher categories].

As for the characteristics of a Bodhisattva, there are those identical to the Buddha’s; they do not belong to the mundane world, and thus are separately described as "transcending. Therefore, it is said to be sixteen.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the lifespan follows that of the devas," etc., a question is raised: Why is it not translated [differently]? The answer is: Because the lifespan has not yet been seen, it would be difficult to restrain the arrogance of others. Question:

How is it that the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are also included within the bodily dimensions? Answer: Because they mostly pertain to the body; the separate mention of the crown and topknot is for the purpose of adornment.
Furthermore, their physical proportions are themselves also part of the marks and signs.
Commentary: Regarding "Śākyavilagna," the following sections are all ornaments upon the crown.

The subsequent commentary on the characters "neng" (capable) and "zhongzhong xian" (variously manifesting) explains these two and three characters respectively. The character for "yìrùzhū" (wish-fulfilling jewel) explains the character "mónní" (maṇi).
Commentary: "Resembling an *yanguī* (extended scepter)" refers to a treasure of this land [China]. It merely takes its shape as the point of comparison; it is not a transliteration.

If translated from that [Indian] perspective, it should be called a "parrot" (*śuka*). It is taken as a metaphor for being red like a parrot’s beak. That which is held by the Son of Heaven is called an *yanguī*, so named because it causes longevity (*yannian*).
Others say it is a "round scepter" (*yuanguī*), referring to its circular shape. I fear there may be an error, and thus I inquire further.

Commentary: Regarding "different from the holy ones' spiritual transformations" (*shénbiàn*): the character above, "different" (*yì*), refers to being distinct from the holy ones; it may be understood as marvelous, extraordinary, or unique.

Furthermore, the character below, "transformation" (*biàn*), refers to their spiritual transformations. Although these are subordinate to the distinction from the holy ones, they are specifically pointed out within the context of spiritual transformations.
As for what is expressed by "spiritual transformations," it reveals that this Bodhisattva dwells serenely in Tuṣita Heaven and is able to constantly [manifest] all...

This is the manifestation of spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*). Furthermore, regarding the appearance of Buddhas and so forth within form (*rūpa*), this reveals that they are essential companions according to the characteristics of phenomena.
Within the true and eternal, nothing is required as a support. The ten wholesome paths and the hundred blessings mutually assist one another to become ten thousand;

the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) are likewise, assisting each other by twos to form ten million, which is one hundred billion. Then, traversing the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they become one hundred [billion].
One *billion* (*koṭi*) consists of ten million. Thus, "color" (*rūpa*) is that *billion*. This refers to self-benefit.

Within the context of benefiting others, because it is more difficult to summon [the result], one reduction is applied, resulting in only one hundred thousand. Furthermore, those one hundred thousand are merely one hundred thousand;

they do not refer to hundreds of thousands of *billion*-eons (*koṭī-kalpa*). There are immeasurable numbers of hundreds of thousands, which also exceed the aforementioned *billion*. This is because benefiting others is superior.

Regarding the sūtra’s statement that they "are made of the colors of a hundred jewels": these are summoned by a hundred merits and represent causing others to act; this is also the same as the thirty-two [marks] of oneself.

Regarding the cultivation of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), there is both a general and a specific classification. The general refers to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), or it may refer to the stages prior to the [ten] grounds (*bhūmi*), as these consist of only those six.
The specific classification divides them into ten; within this division of ten, the first six each have three, while the latter four each have two, totaling thirty-two.
Twelfth: Regarding the causes that bring about [the marks] and those they signify, for both oneself and others, it is the same as previously stated.

Furthermore, among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), the five faculties (*indriya*) and the five powers (*bala*) differ only in name but are identical in essence; since there is no difference in their causal efficacy, these two groups combined constitute five items, resulting in only thirty-two [marks].

Moreover, some say that by practicing the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) within the four modes of birth (*yoni*), or by avoiding the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), one brings forth the thirty-two [marks]; these are the eight [additional marks].
Tenth: because the eight factors of the path assist the ten perfections. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 24, states:
"There are sentient beings in the world who serve eighty deities; the Bodhisattva cultivates the eighty minor marks (aśīty-anuvyañjana). Their characteristics should be understood accordingly;
other things they represent will be explained in the sub-commentary below."
Commentary: "Because of being extremely dignified and handsome" refers to the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*), not the literal expression.
As Nāgārjuna’s verse states: "A foul vessel filled with delicious food does not please the eater; an ugly person preaching the sublime Dharma does not gladden the listener.

Therefore, the precept is established even among those who lack physical faculties; it is not that a teacher’s dignity and beauty are required as a prerequisite for the precepts or as a basis for pride. Question: Since...

Question: Why does such sublime majesty not attract defilement? Answer: On the contrary, there is one excellence: the forty-fourth is "unstained deportment," because it enables those who see it to remain unstained.

Question: As for the four purities, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three foundations of mindfulness, the three ways in which he needs no protection, great compassion, the quality of non-forgetfulness, the permanent eradication of habitual tendencies, and the wondrous wisdom of all modes—these as well...
Question: Why are they not mentioned within the count of one hundred and forty? Answer: Only those factors already fully present within the causal stage are mentioned;
the latter twenty-eight are only fully present at the subsequent stage.

Commentary: "The face is the honored part" constitutes one symbolic representation (*dvāra*). This represents the excellence of these features over those below; the second symbolic representation is understood from the text.

The first section distinguishes the location of manifestation, while the second section distinguishes the formal characteristics; here too there are two symbolic representations, as can be seen in the text.
Commentary: Regarding "radiantly illuminating all phenomena," *jing* (景) means clarity or brilliance. Because it surpasses others such as the sun, it is called "radiantly illuminating. Commentary:
Regarding "the most excellent among all marks" and so forth, the following explains the intent of first citing this partial [description]. There are two pairs, which constitute...
There are two intentions: the first concerns oneself, and the latter concerns others. This is because other marks may also be possessed by those below the noble stages (*ārya*). Question:

Various explanations state that those in the lower stages also partially obtain the thirty-two marks; why then is this alone singled out? Answer: Those [other cases] are mentioned as a general statement regarding partial attainment.
There is no fault in omitting this.

Regarding the thirty-two marks (*lakṣaṇa*): a "mark" is a mark of merit (*puṇya-lakṣaṇa*) and does not concern physical beauty (*śubha*). "Beauty" is physical excellence and does not concern the manifestation of merit.
Therefore, the two are distinct. Although both may occupy the same location [on the body], they do not contradict one another.

Commentary: Regarding "there is no unequal contact": Question. In the sixty-eighth [mark] among those below the excellent marks, his feet are four finger-widths above the ground yet manifest the patterns of the footprints.
How can this mark be called "equal contact"? Answer. It is called "contact" because it manifests upon the ground;
for its influence reaches there, and this [mark] requires a level surface. Accordingly, whether the ground is high or low, the patterns manifest equally and without exception.

Alternatively, among the matters of convenience, there is the requirement for contact and so forth. Question: In the fifteenth section below, the "Seven Places Filled" (*saptasthāna-paripūrṇa*) also mentions having two feet;
how is this distinct from the present case? Answer: The former merely requires being full, whereas the present requires following the ground.

The ground may be high or low, and one treads upon it to make it level. Question: Does this not mean the feet follow the ground? Answer: It simply means making the ground level, or perhaps merely equalizing the force [of the tread]. [Commentary: Both calves.]
It forms the calf. If this character "bó" (膊) refers to the belly, then *eneya* means a golden deer; it is named for its resemblance to that. Regarding the commentary: "The tips all incline upward.
"Tip" (*duān*) means the crown of the head. "Incline" (*mǐ*) means "without. This indicates that the crown of the head is not visible at the top, and [the hair] all curls to the right.
It means "revolving. Furthermore, the *Qieyun* states: "Miman" refers to beautiful complexions; "man" is extended from the top of the head, meaning the color is further beautiful.
That is, this deep blue-black [hair] constitutes a beautiful complexion.

Commentary: Regarding "the neck and both shoulders": the neck refers to the nape of the neck, what is colloquially called the "nape hollow" (*xiàngkō*). The shoulders refer to what is colloquially called the "shoulder pits" (*qióngkēng*).
In the case of a Buddha, these are all full.

Commentary: Regarding the term "shòu-è" (shoulder and armpit), the character for "jiān" (shoulder) is composed of the radicals "bone" (骨) and "zhuān" (專). This "bó" (膊) is explained in the *Wángpiān* as meaning the spreading of a garment;
it should be used interchangeably [with "shòu"]. It refers to the area below the shoulder and above the elbow.
Commentary: "A majestic and full appearance" refers to the second of the two [categories] concerning the body as a whole;
this pertains to having a large face that is upright and straight, whereas others may have it slanted. Alternatively, the latter three characteristics all pertain to the body as a whole.

This eighteenth [characteristic] pertains to being large and straight; the nineteenth pertains to being long and broad; and the twentieth pertains merely to being perfectly circular. *Nyagrodha* means "growing alone."
"Willow" (*liù*) means the body is round and well-proportioned.

"Sparse" (*shū*) refers to one whose majestic appearance is vast; this denotes possessing a powerful presence. It does not refer to formal deportment (*weiyi*), which is distinct from the eighteen [marks].

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the constant light extends one *xun* on each side," this refers to the body’s natural radiance when no supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*) are being performed. This constant bodily light extends for one *xun* on each of the four sides.
One *xun* is eight feet (*chi*); according to the *Qièyùn*, it is six feet, though some say it is one *zhang*.
Commentary: "The four teeth are fresh white and sharp" refers to the front teeth; alternatively, it may refer to them collectively.

This meaning actually refers to the four large back teeth. There are four on each side below. Here, the emphasis is placed on their being fresh white and primarily on their sharpness. "Fresh" means pure.
The white [light] is also present in front.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Because the throat vessel is straight," etc., this explains the reason for obtaining the supreme flavor (*rasāgra*).
Some say that the vital energy vessel located at the side of the throat is called the "throat vessel."
The commentary states: "Like a celestial drum" refers to spring lightning. Regarding the term "elegant and concise": "elegant" (*wan*) means beautiful; "concise" (*yue*) means succinct.
It is like the voice of the *kinnara*; the *kalaviṅka* is a bird of wondrous song.
Commentary: Regarding "like the bow of the Heavenly Emperor," some say it is the bow of Śakra-devānām-indra, while others say it is the rainbow, which is commonly called "the crimson one" (*jiàng*).
Commentary:
Regarding *uṣṇīṣa*, it is said to mean the "golden crown-bone. No one is able to see it.
Commentary: Regarding "fingernails and so forth," there are eight meanings. As for the phrase "like a flower or red copper":
that which emerges from the flesh is naturally [pale], while that which remains within the flesh is crimson, like the color of a red lotus flower or red copper.
Commentary: Regarding "the fingers of the hands and feet," there are seven [points] herein. Commentary:
Regarding "equal and without difference," the dimensions of both hands are equal and without difference; or they are equal as previously described.

As for the fingers, they correspond accordingly, being without difference in size: when combined with large ones, they are large; when combined with small ones, they are small. When the two hands are compared to one another, so too are the feet.
According to this principle, it is not the case that the hand and the foot are said to be equal without distinction.

[The] Commentary states: "Perfect and according to wish" means being complete and without deficiency, like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), whereby one obtains what is needed. This is the sixth [point], shared with the following.
Commentary: Regarding "the sinews and veins are coiled and knotted," this refers to obtaining the mark of the superior flavor (*rasarasāgratā*). The throat-vein is straight;
here, these sinews and veins are like a coiling dragon, hidden and never ceasing its winding.
Commentary: "Advancing straightly with measured step" means not taking crooked steps; it is also a matter of the grand demeanor. Commentary:
"Majestic appearance is uniform and solemn" means that the posture is orderly and not chaotic, naturally bringing tranquility to the ground. Furthermore, "solemn" (su) means respectful.
When one is in a superior position, they are majestic yet respectful; when in an inferior position, they are awe-struck yet affectionate.
Commentary: "Neither excessive nor deficient" means that his steps are neither large nor small, because they are characterized by meditative stability (*samādhi*).
Commentary: "His movements and halts are elegant and refined" means that whether he advances or stops, his deportment is always serene and dignified.

Commentary: Regarding "the entire body follows in rotation," "entire" (*ju*) means pervasive; it does not mean that only the crown of the head rotates. Furthermore, "entire" (*ju*) means movement; the body moves and follows in rotation. Commentary:
Regarding "interlocking without gaps," at the points where they intersect, the interior is knotted and the exterior is filled. This is based on the tenth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
One explanation states: In ordinary people, the joints do not reach one another. In human *mahānagna* (great athletes), the tops of the joints reach one another.
In the body of a *bhadraṅkara*, the various joints are linked together. In the body of a *nārāyaṇa*, the heads of the joints are mutually constrained.

In a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage—that is, the tenth *bhūmi*—the various joint-bones are resolved and bound together like coiled dragons; "constrained" (*ju*) means "tubular" (*guan*), and "bound" (*jie*) means "mutually connected. As for the Buddha:
It is also thus. There are manuscripts where the character *ju* (拘) appears; it is actually the character *gou* (鉤).

Regarding the "hidden place" (*yin chu*), it refers to the great secret organ. It possesses four kinds of excellence. As for "majestic power" (*wei shi*), it means being powerful and intimidating to others.
Commentary: "Dignified and solemn, without fear" means being grave and reverent, always free from apprehension or dread.
Commentary: "Without deficiency" means that whether square or regular, all parts are complete and lacking nothing; furthermore, people do not see it, which means it does not manifest.
Commentary: Regarding "the navel is deep" and so forth, there are six points concerning depth and four points concerning thickness.
Commentary: Regarding defects such as "warts and tumors," those fleshy growths that protrude above the skin and rise up like mounds of earth are called warts; these are simply superfluous flesh.
This is called "redundant" (*zhui*).
Commentary: Regarding "the palms being flat and full," this refers to the seven parts being filled; it does not concern their being level.
Commentary: Regarding "the tongue being symmetrical," this means the tongue is excellent.

Commentary: Regarding the "teeth being even," etc., there are three marks of excellence here; as for the "tusks," there are four marks of excellence. Regarding the term "gradual," it means that the subsequent ones gradually sharpen those preceding them.
Commentary: Regarding the "eyelashes," etc., there are three marks of excellence here.
Commentary: Regarding "the two eyebrows being long and even," there are five marks of excellence here.
Commentary: Regarding "the two eyebrows being elegant and graceful," "graceful" (mi) means beautiful. There are three marks of excellence here.
Commentary: Regarding "thick ears" and so forth, there are four such marks of excellence (*lakṣaṇa*).
Commentary: Regarding "two ears" and so forth, there are three such marks of excellence.
Commentary: Regarding "neither abandoning nor defiling," because one loves [the Buddha] without being defiled, it is called "loving reverence."
Commentary: Regarding "the broad forehead" and so forth, there are four [marks] herein. Commentary:
Regarding "the hair on the head is long," "long" means extended, and "not white" means blue-black. Together, these constitute three secondary marks of excellence (*anuvyañjana*).
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the hair at the crown is fragrant and pure," there are six points of excellence here.
Commentary: "Neat and orderly, neither disheveled nor entangled": to be generally untidy is "disheveled"; for one or two strands to be interwoven is "entangled."
Commentary: *Nārāyaṇa* means "Deity of the Human Race" (*Renzhong Shen*). His body is firm and solid, and he possesses great power. Commentary:
Regarding "countenance relaxed and at ease" (*shutai*) and so forth: *tai* means "unimpeded. To be expansive and free from obstruction is called "relaxed and at ease" (*shutai*).
To stand out from the crowd and be brilliantly manifest is called "radiant and distinguished" (*guangxian*).
Commentary: "Smiling and speaking first" has two meanings: his face is always smiling, never showing an expression of anger;
and when seeing others, he speaks first to offer greetings and inquiries.
Commentary: "Facing only forward and not turning back" means that when people come from the four directions, they all see him facing them.
Commentary: Regarding *tāla* (or *dāna*) of the Tathāgata, the *Jīng yīnyì* (Meanings and Pronunciations of the Sūtras) states:

*madana*, or *mathana*, is translated here as "intoxicating fruit. Eating this fruit can cause a person to become intoxicated. Its shape is round and exquisite, resembling the head of Śakra; it is as large as a cartwheel.
The fruit is like a celestial canopy; "celestial" refers to a heavenly parasol.
Regarding the commentary on the phrase "the body hairs are deep blue" (*gāndhārī*): among the deep blue, there is a radiant luster, interspersed with reddish hues as an ornamental embellishment.

Commentary: "According to the size of the assembly" means that when there are many people, [the voice] is small. Furthermore, according to the capacity of the listeners, the words contain nothing superfluous and all accord with reason.

Regarding the "low and high" mentioned below, it follows the measure of each individual person, causing their minds to be harmonious and joyful. The following seventy-two [points] concern the meaning of what is desired;
the following concerns the substance of the sound.

Commentary: Regarding "his feet were raised from the ground," "raised" means separated. Within the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*, there are three meanings for the explanation that [the feet] did not touch the ground:

first, because there were insects; second, because there was living grass; and third, to manifest supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) at a height of four finger-widths, signifying separation from the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*).
Furthermore, the manifestation of wheel patterns signifies the turning of the Wheel of Dharma. This is because the Tathāgata’s feet are so pristine. Thus says the Sūtra.
There are three conditions: first, to cause people to have few desires; second, to manifest the marks of the wheel; third, so that people see them and rejoice. Regarding the commentary:
"meandering" (weiyi) signifies being weak or slight, or else it refers to the appearance of arrogance.
Commentary: "Always young and never aging" means that Śākyamuni always appears as if he were twenty-five years old.
Commentary: "Loves to visit former sites" means that an old man does not like to linger in old places; he mostly abandons them all.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "possessing auspicious joyous swirls," this does not refer to the *svastika* nor to the thousand-spoked wheels; rather, there are distinct swirling patterns that inspire joy in those who see them, hence they are called "joyous swirls.
See the fifty-seventh treatise in the eleventh fascicle of the *Za lun* (Compendium). These are among the various marks and signs of excellence.

The bases of the four faculties—namely, the body, the male organ, the tongue, and the eye—are distinct in their essential nature. That which attains the supreme taste is so called because it is the "supreme object" (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, the sound of the Dharma is also subsumed under the bases of the faculties, as it is an internal sound.

Question: When examining the marks (*lakṣaṇa*), the ears and nose are absent; yet they are present within the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). Now, in this compiled text, you have fully explained both the marks and the secondary characteristics. Why is this?

It does not say "two. The answer, "the nose is straight and so forth," refers only to external appearance; it is merely the support for the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), not the support for the ear- or nose-faculties.

The support for the faculties that are included therein is co-spatial with the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Alternatively, this may be a general statement; however, its characteristics are not auspicious.

The five bases (*āśraya*) are well-established; when the spheres (*dhātu*) are expanded, they become six. Question: Why does the male organ (*vyañjana-indriya*) lack a corresponding *paramārtha* (ultimate) sense-faculty? Answer:

It merely takes up its formal characteristics (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*), but it does not necessarily take up its object (*viṣaya*). Question: As for things such as body hair and nails, why are they considered bases of faculties (*indriyāśraya*) exclusively? Answer:

While they are nominally designated as such, in reality they belong to the category of external matter (*bāhya-rūpa*). However, they are also termed internal matter (*ādhyātma-rūpa*). Here, we are referring to the category of internal matter; thus, they are all called bases of faculties. This is based on the twenty-two faculties (*dvāviṃśati-indriya*).
The middle section clarifies this. Therefore, the boundaries and faculties are opened. In the commentary:
“Subhūti, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha,” and so forth, down to the character “therefore” (故), concludes the preceding and gives rise to what follows.
Within that which is produced, there is first light and then sound. Within these lights and sounds, each speaks of its own functional manifestation. Its...
Its magnitude is extremely vast. Subsequently, when one discerns this according to the capacities of beings, its magnitude is reduced.
As for the statement that it "spontaneously illuminates the trichiliocosm," this is also said provisionally in accordance with the manifestation of a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Its subsequent mental attention is likewise a characteristic of transformation. Question: Since it follows the characteristics of transformation, a minor transformation would only illuminate the four continents.

How does it spontaneously illuminate the great trichiliocosm? Answer: Whether it be a great transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), a reward body Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya*), or a small transformation body, the capacity of the sentient being is such that there is no loss of light, even at a great distance.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "Such merits as those of Subhūti," this further reveals his excellence. It praises the fruit by citing the cause;
because he has already attained these causes in the past and the Buddha has further attained them, he is thus superior. This is clearly evident from the first bhūmi upward.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "In this way, Subhūti," etc., the following section again summarizes and returns to the Prajñāpāramitā.
Since it is within the Prajñāpāramitā that one cultivates these two [qualities] and thereby attains them, this is the marvelous and extraordinary dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the thirty-two marks arise from the cultivation of practices" and so forth: the above constitutes the text explaining the specific characteristics (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa);

what follows below is the text explaining the general characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa). Within the sūtra, each of the marks and secondary signs (anuvyañjana) possesses five hundred *koṭis* of colors and eighty-four thousand clouds of radiant light.
However, in the current commentary, regarding the marks, it describes their precious colors, and regarding the secondary signs—

In the middle [section], it speaks of "clouds of radiant splendor. This is a concise manifestation of the signs; one may infer the rest accordingly. Furthermore, while the sūtra speaks of the "color of the jewels," the commentary (*śāstra*) refers to them as "light" within its summary;
thus, what corresponds to the color of the jewels is precisely the color of the light. Question: What is the difference between this and the *ūrṇā-lakṣaṇa* (the hair-tuft mark)?
Moreover, regarding that *ūrṇā-lakṣaṇa*, which is among the thirty-two marks, it was previously stated to be "hundredfold," and subsequently again...
Regarding the statement "five," the answer is as follows: The *ūrṇā* mark is preeminent, radiating distinct rays of light that surpass all other colors; these rays number five hundred billion.
Furthermore, there are those within the marks that possess only color, which likewise number five hundred.

Thus, they are not identical. Nevertheless, these jewel-colors may also be called "light," though they do not manifest repeatedly. Together with the ten wholesome deeds (*daśa-kuśala*), which assist one another, they constitute one hundred. Combined—
By performing these practices oneself and so forth, they become one thousand. A thousand times, with two thousand assisting each time, results in one million.

Within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one cultivates one million in each; this constitutes ten million, which forms one hundred million (*koṭi*). Upon reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), one again cultivates one million.
By means of this one million, all that was previously cultivated throughout the ten stages is augmented, resulting in one hundred billion (*koṭi-koṭi*). Thus it is.
Furthermore, practicing according to the five modes of cultivation constitutes five million billion causes.

Moreover, within this context, because one is free from arrogance (*māna*), the mark of the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the tuft of hair between the eyebrows) preeminently manifests in the colors of a hundred jewels. Among those things abandoned, pride assists the other primary afflictions;
as they mutually support one another to form ten, and since there are likewise one hundred instances of "acting for oneself" and so forth, [the total reaches one hundred].

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the gates of the various pāramitās," the meaning of the text is easily understood. Furthermore, there are cases where they are accumulated solely by way of the dharma-gates:

for example, as it is said regarding the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karma-patha*). Since the ten wholesome actions mutually complete one another, this already constitutes one hundred; when explaining their self-performance and so forth, this likewise constitutes one thousand.
Self-benefit and benefit for others together constitute two thousand; adding the total of one hundred, they become two thousand and one hundred.

In this manner, those in the desire realm—those of the six destinies and four modes of birth—as well as those in the eight concentrations of the upper realms, including the initial threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate dhyānas, are thus delivered.

When these are fully established, there are ten types within the supramundane realm: the four candidates for the fruits [of stream-entry], the four fruits themselves, the causal stage of the pratyekabuddha, and the ten stages of the bodhisattva.
Thus, they collectively constitute eighty-four thousand. Although this is not explicitly stated in the scriptural texts, it is logically tenable.

Furthermore, regarding those who maintain that [the afflictions] are explained solely in relation to the afflictions themselves: based on the ten root afflictions, when they mutually assist one another, they form one hundred; including their preceding and succeeding phases, they thus become three hundred.
By dividing the middle portion, it assists the preceding and succeeding parts; the preceding and succeeding portions each become one thousand. Thus, together they total two thousand and one hundred.
To these four classes of sentient beings, the four great elements and the six bases of decay (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are added to accumulate their number.

Furthermore, upon the two thousand and one hundred, there are four thousand and two hundred—both those already arisen and those yet to arise—and additionally, two thousand secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

The afflictions are thus assisted; in this manner, they also total eighty-four thousand. There is further meaning, as found in the *Fayuan chao* (Excerpts from the Garden of the Dharma) and its commentary.
Regarding "radiance": when he first descended from Tuṣita, his light illuminated ten billion sets of four great continents and so forth.
Commentary: Regarding "representing the assembly of Bodhisattvas," this refers to the great assembly of Maitreya. This assembly comprises those of the Three Vehicles and the Two Vehicles.

In terms of emerging from the mud of afflictions—which is what is meant by "birth and death"—the previous mention of sitting upon lotuses symbolizes that the Bodhisattvas have emerged from the Two Vehicles.
Furthermore, regarding the "mud" of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), it is also based on the lower causes; thus, there is no contradiction.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "three times by day and three times by night," these two clauses distinguish the characteristics [of the practice], which will be clarified in the following text.

This does not mean that one should perform six separate sessions at different times; rather, it means being present throughout all six periods. Since one does not remain idle during these six periods, practitioners today must not merely complete six recitations and then cease;
they must remain uninterrupted throughout day and night. Even when one is utterly exhausted, one should pause only briefly.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "causing the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) and so forth to arise," this refers to that which is manifested. According to what was stated previously, why would the nine hundred million devaputras not have something manifested?
Therefore, through ten thousand myriad practices across the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and by means of the five faculties and so forth, these disciples are attained.

Commentary: Regarding the signs of falling asleep, there is another explanation which states that day and night are distinguished by the blooming and closing of flowers and the singing and silence of birds and beasts.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that for birds and beasts born from eggs, once they die and their carcasses are left behind, before long a violent wind will blow them away and transport them to another location.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* says this is a transformation (*nirmāṇa*). This concludes the supplementary explanation according to other schools.
Regarding "the elephant and so forth," they do not know the place of death.
[The] Commentary states: "The Buddha is not like this" means that even in what appears to be sleep, there is no such state;

this is because Maitreya refers to the Buddha as one who never dwells [in stillness] throughout the six periods of the day and night. This accords with the character *heng* (constant) in the sutra. Based on these six periods, it does not refer merely to six cycles.
Commentary: Regarding the "one hundred forty-four billion years" mentioned here, one hundred million is termed a "billion" (億), and this is the number obtained.
As for the calculation of "five thousand seven hundred and sixty billion" below, this is likewise calculated based on ten million being a "billion."
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "Now, by means of reasoning... and so forth, this section below provides a reconciliation and explanation, which is presented in two parts.

First, it is based on the calculation of the great *mahāsaṃkhyā* (great number), wherein one hundred is treated as one. For example, when counting *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, ten winds (*vāyu*) are treated as one wind;

thus, there is this reconciliation where one hundred is taken as one. Ten thousand is then termed a *koṭi* (billion); this is precisely equivalent to treating one million as a *koṭi*, and the terminology corresponds exactly.
"Those whose large numbers correspond [are such that] even six characters still differ; as will be revised and added below, they should be reconciled according to this in the subsequent explanation.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, 'By reasoning through the principles, one calculates ten million as a hundred million,' etc.: Question: Since this principle already exists, why was it necessary to provide the previous explanation for reconciliation?
Answer: Above the character 'wan' (ten thousand) in the passage below, one must add six characters; otherwise, there would still be a deficiency of one hundred characters."

The six characters are then moved to be above the character "wan" (萬). However, since the number is already complete with the character "yi" (億) having seven characters, it is preferable to move them because fewer characters need to be altered.
This constitutes the previous explanation. Furthermore, below, one again follows the previous method by adding and altering characters.
However, the original intent of the sutra lies in its later interpretation. In the West (India), ten million is commonly regarded as one hundred million (*koṭi*).

Thus, when the Bodhisattva Precepts speak of "one thousand, ten thousand, and ten million Śākyamunis," this is based on the convention of taking ten million as a hundred million; it refers precisely to a *koṭi*.
Regarding the explanation of the Hīnayāna, it mostly relies on the *lakṣa*, which is one hundred thousand (*śatasahasra*).

In the commentary (*śūtra*), it states that the character "wan" (ten thousand) should have the character "zhe" (one) placed above it; this, however, merely shifts the character based on the former interpretation.

If one follows the latter interpretation, ten million is a *koṭi*, and thus the character "wan" should properly have the character "bai" (hundred) added above it. Furthermore, since this can be inferred from other sources, it is omitted here for brevity, as it would be too concise otherwise.
One hundred and five million. If one follows the latter interpretation, it would be short by one hundred and five million.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "This takes ten million as one *koṭi*," this actually follows the former system, which treats a hundred as one and one million as a *koṭi*;
such is its method of calculation. If one were to take only a single ten million as a *koṭi*, it would precisely accord with the aforementioned commentary on this sutra.

This is because ten thousand are treated as one; thus, they are cited to illustrate this principle. Subsequently, a single unit is treated as one, and ten thousand times ten thousand is reckoned as a hundred million (*koṭi*).
As for the statement that although the increments and decrements differ, they are equivalent:
while the calculation of the *koṭi* differs, it does not involve adding or shifting [digits], and thus it accords exactly with the mathematical algorithms of the treatises.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "those six hundred million," etc., from this point downward, one intends to change "thousand" (千) to "hundred" (百).
This directly reveals the contradiction; there is no need to explicitly state that it is a correction, for people will understand it themselves. Question: How is there a contradiction? Answer:

Because one sees that the lower positions are the same as the upper, which are designated as "hundreds of millions" (億); yet the upper positions are only five hundred and sixty million, whereas the calculation for the lower positions results in six hundred million.

Because it is a *yì* (billion). Furthermore, since they are both *yì*, why not simply state "one hundred and sixteen *yì* years"? Thus, the character for "thousand" (*qiān*) here is actually the character for "hundred" (*bǎi*).
If one were to claim that an "upper *yì*" (*shàng yì*) is ten million (*wànwàn*), then since ten million constitutes an *yì*, [the number] would not yet reach fifty;
it would merely be five. Therefore, it is only fifty-seven *chíwàn* (ten million) years, and does not reach fifty-seven *wànwàn* (hundred million).
Therefore, if one were to say that ten million constitutes a hundred million (*koṭi*), then the six hundred million in the lower position would also suffice for the calculation in the upper position.
The reason the Master of the Commentary refutes [the opponent] by taking one million as a hundred million is because he had not previously taken ten thousand times ten thousand (*wan-wan*) as such;
furthermore, taking *wan-wan* would instead refute the upper position. Thus, he takes only one million as a hundred million, for the meaning of the term is not [otherwise established].

Regarding "contradiction": because they are utterly contradictory, it is a term that reverses "harmony. If this lower rank is likewise one hundred million, would it not be non-contradictory to be greater than the higher rank?
This is a correction of two characters; even so, it remains utterly contradictory.
Because it is utterly contradictory, such a passage—or these semantic characters—lacks the character "豈" (qǐ). Above, following the commentary, I have distinguished the essentials of the sutra. If...
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the calculation establishing that one lifetime in the heavens of the six classes of gods is equivalent to a certain number of human years is as follows:
for the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*), it is nine million human years—where ten million is a "koṭi" (billion)—but not yet reaching one hundred million.

As one proceeds upward through the higher realms, the number is calculated by multiplying by four each time, which precisely accords with those figures. Thus, nine million multiplied by four [results in thirty-six million]. Four.
Nine times thirty-six million years is three hundred and sixty million years. Since ten million is a *koṭi* (billion), this amounts to three hundred and sixty million years.
This is the lifespan of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Furthermore, by multiplying that by four, it is the lifespan of the Yāma Heaven:
one billion four hundred and forty million years. Again, by multiplying that by four, it is the [lifespan] of the Tuṣita Heaven: fifty...

Seventy-six million years. This is the lifespan of Maitreya while dwelling in the heavens; thus, the commentary adds the character "seven" and shifts the characters "six" down, yet it still omits one hundred characters from the current text.
Furthermore, by four causes, this is the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, with a lifespan of twenty-three billion four hundred million years.
Again, by four causes, this is the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, [with a lifespan of] nine hundred twenty-one... [billion years].
One hundred and sixty million years; in this sequence, one day and one night shall pass within each of the first six hells.
This is according to the Buddha’s teaching: when a Buddha appears in the world, the lifespan of human beings increases accordingly.
However, if we compare this to the present, or even to the time when the human lifespan is ten years, both the days and the years decrease by an even greater number than that reduction.

At the beginning of a kalpa, the lifespan and the duration of the days are both so long that they cannot be measured by such numbers; therefore, for the latter two hells, the kalpa is reckoned not by years but by [the duration of] two earth-hells.
In the seventh hell, it lasts for half an increasing-and-decreasing kalpa (*antara-kalpa*). This time has already passed beyond that of the sixth hell;
otherwise, it would directly contradict the *Yogācārabhūmi*, which states that the lifespan increases progressively in the lower realms. The same applies to the body size.
However, it is asked: When Maitreya is born in heaven, this human world passes through the period from a lifespan of one hundred years decreasing to ten years for seven thousand years;

then, from ten years, when the sons' ages double those of their fathers, increasing until the lifespan reaches eighty-four thousand years—though this duration is not fixed, the number of years is not many—and then, from eighty-four thousand years, it decreases back to eighty thousand years. This is merely a decrease.
Four thousand [years] decrease by one every century. Four thousand multiplied by one hundred is four hundred thousand.
Thus, the number of human years that pass during the lifespan of Maitreya in heaven is fixed at exactly four hundred and seven thousand.

Although the number for the increasing eons (*vivartakalpa*) is not yet fixed, it cannot exceed the number of decreasing eons (*saṃvartakalpa*). Even when calculating the total of the decreasing eons, they do not reach one hundred million. How so?
It can last for many years. Answer: This has already been explained as before. When the lifespan in the heavens reaches one hundred years, it is five billion seven hundred and sixty million years.
Regarding those who pass through the kalpas, when the lifespan increases to eighty-four thousand years, this is because the months and days at that time are extremely long.
Although the rule was once that the lifespan decreased by one year per century, it also decreases by one hundred days [per century].
Regarding "one day": at the time of the beginning of that kalpa, one day was equivalent to what is here [in this world] a hundred years.
For two years and some odd months, it was like this every single day; thus, when calculated accurately, it does not amount to much.

However, taking the full duration as a hundred years, it is five billion seven hundred and sixty million years. Question: Is the full lifespan of the other *paranirmita-vaśavartin* gods equal to the lifespan of the sixth hell?
One day and one night. In that sixth hell, the full lifespan is sixteen thousand [years]. In the seventh hell, it is half an *antara-kalpa* (intermediate kalpa).
How can such a vast number of years be calculated? Answer: During the increasing kalpa (*vivarta-kalpa*), the years likewise increase accordingly; it is roughly like this.
A detailed calculation will follow later, but I have not yet had the leisure to compute it. This is the duration of the lifespan in the seventh hell.
[The text] divides [the lifespan]. It must exceed the sixth [heaven].
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'the Bodhisattva being in the heavens,' etc.," it is because one fears an external objection might claim:

"Even if there is a reduction of one hundred and five million years, there is no fault, for he does not descend to be born below until his celestial lifespan is exhausted. This is used to refute that [objection], as there is no such thing as premature death [among the gods].
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "born among humans," some versions read "born in the human realm. This interpretation connects the meaning with the preceding section.

Following this version, the current sentence is connected to what follows, marking his birth among humans. According to the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, this shall occur when the human lifespan reaches sixty thousand years.
When their lifespan in the heavens comes to an end, they descend to be born among humans; Maitreya is likewise.
At that time, the human lifespan will be sixty thousand years—unlike the time of Śākyamuni, when it was but eighty years.

As for the statement that he appears at a time when humans have long lifespans, it is because those of long life are fit to behold Maitreya; thus he manifests according to the requirements of that time. Regarding the years mentioned in this sutra:

It is too few. The *Tāishòu jīng* (Sūtra on Dwelling in the Womb) states eighty-four thousand [kalpas]; furthermore, the number of kalpas is too many. Therefore, both are rejected together; there is no need for reconciliation.

Regarding the passage in the sūtra where the Buddha addresses Upāli and others: the text is abbreviated and does not conclude with the description of the descent into birth, as it is primarily explaining the ascent to birth.
This is because it speaks of the lower [realms].

As for the passage in the Sūtra concerning "after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa": while the Buddha was still present, beings were necessarily devoted to the Buddha; therefore, he caused them to practice in the present life, and at the end [of his teaching], he exhorted them to seek rebirth [in the Pure Land].
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "exhorting them to be born there," in the previous section on external fruits, it was first shown that those born as humans lack such aspirations;
here, however, there is no mention of those who are born there. Thus, the two passages correspond to one another.
Commentary: Although there are five sections and so forth, from here below, they are separately categorized and explained in three segments.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "In the first [of these], there are six," within each of the three segments among the aforementioned five sections, the first segment is further divided into six sub-sections.

Commentary: First, regarding "diligence," it is so called because it universally exerts effort toward all dharmas. The scriptural passage provides the general heading, while the commentary follows by citing its specific components.

The essential point is the phrase "to cultivate all meritorious virtues" (*puṇya*), which constitutes one practice. Here, the term "merit" (*guṇa*) is a designation for the fruit; what is currently being cultivated is the causal practice.
Because the cause receives the name of the fruit, this is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (possessive compound). It is not that the word "merit" refers to the form of the cause itself.
Regarding what is called "cultivation" (bhāvanā), it applies equally to the giving of robes and so forth; all such acts are termed the cultivation of merit.

Therefore, the text uses the plural "various. The commentary states that among the two fields—the field of compassion and the field of reverence—the karma performed therein still possesses the sense of "equality."

Since "benefit" (*anugraha*) is included within "respect" (*satkāra*), these three fields (*kṣetra*) encompass everything; thus, they are broad and comprehensive. By this general classification, they constitute "giving" (*dāna*);
while the initial heading provides the general designation, it thereby acquires its specific names.

Commentary: Regarding the third point, "sweeping stupas and smearing the ground," this mentions sweeping and smearing as representative acts; the construction [of stupas] and so forth are all included therein.
Therefore, the commentary states "organizing the caityas" (制多) and adds the word "etc. (等). This sweeping of stupas and other such acts fall under the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

By causing others to rejoice, one practices patience without anger and thereby personally attains the merit of patience. For instance, selling alcohol constitutes the karma of frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*). Its...
Regarding those who drink alcohol: because they engage in frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*), those who sell it cause them to incur the karma of frivolous speech.

This is from the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*. In the commentary, regarding the "four types of offerings of incense and flowers": "incense and flowers" refers to the specific items, while "offerings" is the general category.

Therefore, the commentary explains these as the four requisites. These four requisites are clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine; "requisites" (*pariṣkāra*) refers to all other [necessities].
Objects of enjoyment, up to and including dwellings, all receive this name. "Shi" (什) means "various. Because there are many phenomena and characteristics, the practice is characterized by diligence.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The five types of ordinary persons' practices, the various samādhis, and so forth": first, it explains that ordinary persons generally attain both distracted states and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), as well as their cultivation.

The "higher concentration" (ūrdhvadhyāna) refers to the six types of practice, including the general characteristic mindfulness (*sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛti*) and so forth; thus, the character "etc. (*ādi*) appears after "hearing and reflection" (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī*).

The noble cultivation of the untainted (*anāsrava*) is called "right reception" (*samyaksamādhi*); "right" (*samyañc*) means "noble," because it is untainted. Regarding the noble tainted concentration (*āryasāsravadhyāna*), it may occur either before or after [the higher concentration].
As for the second interpretation: the noble cultivation is the same as before, while for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the cultivation of the higher [stages] is excluded.

Regarding "concentration" (*samādhi*): it refers to the fact that the names of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the three types of cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā*), *samādhi*, and *samāpatti* are common [to all].
Regarding the commentary’s mention of "reciting and chanting the scriptures": while the sutra mentions only recitation and chanting, the commentary adds "explaining and expounding" as well.
Regarding the practice of the ten dharmas within the teachings, all are contained herein; therefore, this is the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

[The] Commentary states: "As for the mention of 'six matters' and so forth, these are cited as representative instances of excellence, or because they are easy to practice. Generally speaking, they are the foremost because they are accessible," and so on.
The Commentary has already added that there are many further details both internal and external.

Commentary: Regarding the statement "if one fully cultivates the six perfections," a question arises: since the commentary itself explains the method for classifying the grades [of practitioners], could those who lack the precepts still be born [in the Pure Land]?
Among those who cultivate five of the perfections, with each of the five excluding one, there is necessarily at least one person among them who lacks the precepts.
The Sūtra states: "If a person does not receive the precepts, even a mange-scarred wild jackal cannot obtain [this body], let alone one endowed with complete merit.

Answer: The various masters each offer their own interpretations, and no explicit textual authority has been seen. Now, I shall provide a single coherent interpretation to explain the reason for this.
This division into six is based on the primary practice; according to what serves as the primary factor, there are six, five, and so forth, up to only one.
One takes the primary practice as the main focus, while the other practices come to assist it; in this way, one is still said to be practicing only "one practice.
Through these primary and auxiliary practices together, one can summon that celestial realm and attain birth there.

Were it otherwise, there would certainly be no possibility of birth, for the matter of such karmic fruition is not a minor one. According to what has been explained above, the Inner Court and the Outer Palaces are like eyes.
It is seen that [the result] cannot be obtained from a single cause alone. How, then, can it be experienced through a single cause? Question:

Is it not taught by the Buddha that many fruits arise from few causes? Answer: It is indeed possible for there to be few causes and many fruits within a single category, according to what is appropriate;
however, this does not mean that a single cause brings about multiple categories [of results]. For example, one who possesses no ethical discipline but practices only generosity will bring about—
How noble! Thus, those devas are indeed noble; they possess everything such as clothing, food, and attendants.
What single factor could have brought about all this? Therefore, within that state, one may distinguish between the primary and the secondary;
even at the time of enjoyment, one distinguishes between guest and host, and there are relations of superiority and inferiority. All such things are explained in terms of their causes, as follows:
Within these three major sections of the lower grade, according to what is explained here, and further discussing them by means of the nine grades, their characteristics are likewise thus.

These nine grades mutually function as both primary and secondary; they should be complete according to their respective applications, or perhaps have some omissions, yet they must not be entirely lacking.
According to the aforementioned commentary, each one among them fully encompasses all practices, which constitutes being "complete within the secondary."
The middle and lower [capacities] have been explained. Do not focus exclusively on a single practice, lest you fall into error.

Furthermore, those who focus solely on visualization and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) are establishing something quite hollow. According to the scriptural text below, each and every practice is a matter of observing and inducing [realization] during the time of cultivation without fail.
Why, then, would there be another teaching that claims visualization alone is the primary method?
It is called the "correct cause" because all virtues take faith as their primary guide. However, how could it be that all karmic fruits take faith alone as their correct cause?

Therefore, one should understand this through the teachings on "contemplation according to one's wishes" and the like. It is called the "guide" because it serves as the leader for directing [the practitioner];
it is not itself the correct cause. Those who seek rebirth should cultivate and contemplate this; do so correctly and do not contemplate it in vain, lest you fall into error.
It is also empty.
Regarding the scriptural passage, "Such persons as these," this phrase must refer back to those who practice the six modes of conduct.
It instructs them to apply their minds with sincerity and even to fix their mindfulness. How could it be that the contemplation of emptiness concerns things such as the *dou* and *liang* measures?
Regarding the sūtra on "contemplating the physical form [of the Buddha]," this refers in advance to Maitreya; we shall now invoke him. This is also the time for practice:
one should visualize his appearance according to one's capacity through general characteristics, without needing to measure it down to the smallest dimensions.
If one were required to be complete in every detail, even contemplating just a single crown for many years would not suffice—how much less so for a body sixteen *yojanas* tall? Thirty... [text ends].
The two marks and eighty minor characteristics—such majestic perfection as this would never be exhausted throughout the ages. How, then, can it be brought about through cultivation?
Therefore, one must fix the mind according to one's capacity and not allow it to wander toward other objects, for such practice would otherwise be reckless and unsteady.
The practitioner must reflect so as not to expend effort in vain; thus, the commentary states: "Even though one practices, one must still..."
Right mindfulness. The mind also draws forth thoughts based on one's conduct; it is not merely a matter of remaining upright and still. [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "not violating at other times," the first two phrases serve as a negation of what is improper, while the third phrase provides the formal explanation. Having received the precepts, one maintains them or violates them.
In the sutras, it appears that even the power of maintaining them for a single moment can bring about results; it is not the case that one immediately commits a violation after that single moment.
They attain birth. Furthermore, there is no fixed vow or single thought by which one receives [birth]; this is merely a provisional illustration.
This sutra has cited one example from each of the upper and lower grades; as for the remaining lower grade and the other two grades, they are clearly demonstrated [elsewhere].
The Sūtra says: "For example, like a strong man who has the power to bend and extend [his limbs] so swiftly that it takes but a moment.
"Bending and extending" carries the meaning of contracting and stretching. Just as a powerful strong man bends and extends his arms, in such a brief moment, one is reborn there.
Commentary: "Having already been born in those heavens" and so forth indicates purity.
Sūtra: "Extensively cultivating meritorious deeds. In the previous section on exhortation to practice, a single thought-moment was cited as a provisional example to facilitate compliance;

here, in this section of praise, the phrase "extensively cultivating" is used to inspire joy. Even a single thought-moment may be termed "extensive," for it is the aspiration of the mind [that matters].
Because it is great. A single thought-moment constitutes a vow to be born in many vast [lands]. The Sūtra states:
"One immediately attains transcendence of the offenses of birth and death for ninety billion kalpas. This is because it is the very beginning of practice;
by means of the superior encompassing the inferior, and because it possesses the power of the nine grades, one thereby transcends the offenses of ninety billion kalpas. Question: Only...

[Question: One sees nine [kalpas]; how then can there be ten billion? [Answer: Because this is the root of ten million practices, the destruction of sins is likewise ten millionfold, as previously stated.
[Question: What constitutes a kalpa here? Furthermore, does the sinner fall into the three miserable realms (trāya), or do they transcend them?
If they do not exist [in those realms], how is it so? Moreover, since there were previously ninety billion transgressions, one should not take birth; what are their characteristics like?

Question: What is meant by this? Answer: To explain these words now: the offenses of birth and death do not necessarily entail the three miserable realms (*trāya*). All *sāsrava* (outflowing) phenomena constitute birth and death.
From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, one undergoes various cycles of coming and going; the extent of these cycles is what is referred to here.

As for the term "transcending" (*vyutkrānta*), it is like Śākyamuni Buddha encountering Puṣya and others; such cases are called "transcending. This refers to attaining Buddhahood while still encompassing the passage through birth and death.
Regarding the origin [of this statement]: seeing that Maitreya has reduced [the duration of suffering] by such a time. This term "kalpa" (劫) generally refers to the periods of increase and decrease.

Thus, it does not mean that the Bodhisattva Maitreya has transcended ninety billion kalpas of birth and death; all subsequent mentions of "transcending" should be explained according to this principle.
Question: In the commentary (*shu*), you yourself explain the offenses of the hells; why then do you speak here of "all birth and death"? Answer: The commentary...

The mention of suffering is intended to cause people to fear it and to desire its cessation while seeking that [state of liberation]. In reality, however, all [suffering] is that which must be transcended.

If this were not so, would there not be ghosts and animals among those things to be transcended? Alternatively, this may refer specifically to the transcendence of the offenses of the three miserable realms;
this shall be examined further below.
Commentary: In other places, the years of the kalpas of retribution are used as the measure; in the Hell of Intense Heat (*Tapana*), it is likewise half an intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
Because it does not reach the duration of a full kalpa, the term "years" is used by association.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "ordinary beings of the final kalpa," one asks: since the time is that of the lowest of ordinary beings, how can they thus transcend birth and death?

The two phrases [of the commentary] are concessive, while the seven characters "末" (final) through "等" (etc. constitute the conclusion. Within this, there are two refutations: first, regarding the excellence of their practice; second, regarding the power of the object.
In the first "Seizing" (duō), two lines serve as the heading. The term "Pure Land" (Jìngfāng) refers to Tuṣita. The following two lines provide the reasoning to establish this.
"Sù" means early and also respectful; here it takes the sense of "respectful. "Niányùn" means destiny (life-span). "Dān" means exhausted.
This line expresses self-congratulation, while the next line completes the argument. The intended meaning is: [I] respect my destiny and life-span, and...
Because it is inexhaustible, one attains the superior grade and transcends the inferior. The text concludes by asking: "How could it not transcend the offenses of birth and death?

It is like the saying that Heaven leaves no path for man to be cut off; thus, one attains the practice of the superior and inferior grades, and is therefore able to transcend the offenses of birth and death for ninety billion kalpas.
The second section below [deals with] "subtraction"; the text may be considered accordingly. Question: This can extinguish offenses.
Why is it not included in the fifth major section? Furthermore, what is the difference between the meaning of "this" and "that" gate? Answer:
These are all expedient expressions and do not contradict one another; moreover, this refers to the benefit at the time of birth.
[Sūtra]: "Those who do not regress from the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment. This refers, for the time being, to the great stage; in reality, it applies to all three vehicles. [Commentary]:

"According to their respective stages" refers to the five types of non-retrogression. According to their respective stages, among those who have already generated [the aspiration], they cause it to become firm, which is termed "accomplishment."
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the three karmas are all pure," this refers to the middle-upper and the highest-of-the-high levels, as it speaks of them being "all" purified together.

Commentary: "Practicing the six dharmas accordingly" refers to the middle and lower grades within the upper three grades. "The three karmas are slightly purified" refers to the lower grade within the middle three grades.
By the word "slight," each case is shown to be distinct; they are not the standard for the upper grade, yet they generally follow it.

And as for "few," it does not mean they are excluded; thus, each category encompasses both. It does not mention the "inferior" because there is uncertainty regarding them, which shall be understood when we reach that section below.

Furthermore, this indicates that where there is a superior grade, there must necessarily be a middle grade; therefore, it is stated in this way. The characteristics of the inferior grade have already been fully detailed within the [respective] chapters.
Commentary: "Praying with the mind for non-duality" means that non-duality is suchness (*tathatā*). To reveal the Mahāyāna: Commentary:
"The way of father and son still moves Heaven naturally" refers to the natural disposition (*prakṛti*). It does not depend on instruction or exhortation; they follow one another naturally.

How much more so in this matter, where [the Buddha] will certainly descend in accordance [with his vow]. Why would he need to be moved? This is the principle that a shadow does not require external effort to emerge.
The *Bianyin* (Discrimination of Causes) states that this is self-evident.

The *Shu* (Commentary) says: "Regarding 'the six matters of practice being fulfilled,' etc.: [the categories] are 'superior-superior' and 'superior-middle. One would expect that hearing the Dharma at the first assembly should exceed other grades;

yet it is not known how so. Now, I fear that the superior grade must necessarily possess the three karmas and is exclusively of the superior type, such that one hears the Dharma at the first assembly."
Regarding the phrase "before all Buddhas" and so forth in the Sūtra, this refers generally to the Bhadrakalpa, as indicated by the commentary itself.
Regarding the phrase "in the Lesser Vehicle it is said" and so forth in the commentary, the citations provided below vary in length; however, they serve merely as corroborative examples.

Since encountering the Buddhas during the two kalpas is not a matter of one's spiritual stage (*caryā-bhūmi*), there is no need to further explain the principle behind these variations in length. Now...
To summarize: their teachings differ and their numerical reckonings vary. These differences arise from adapting to capacities and following specific intentions; thus, they are not in error.
As for those of the Hīnayāna, they follow the provisional transformations and manifest appearances, and cannot be harmonized with this [ultimate teaching].
Commentary: Regarding "practicing the four reliances," within the Mahāyāna there are the four reliances of the Dharma, namely: relying on the Dharma and not on the person, and so forth.
There are also the four reliances of practice, which are those listed here. Within the Hīnayāna, there are the reliances of practice;
these are: first, relying on regular meals; second, rag-robes; third, dwelling in cemeteries; and fourth, decomposed medicines. These are the four for that person.

Regarding these: among the fruits of the path, there are four—namely, the fruit of the preparatory stage (*prayoga-phala*), the first fruit (*srota-āpanna*), the two intermediate fruits, and the two fruits of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Such are the four. Now, in this Mahāyāna, one does not manifest the four types of persons, but speaks only of their practices. As for what is called "reliance," it means relying on oneself and causing others to all obtain benefit.
Commentary: Regarding the four types of *vyākaraṇa* (prophecies), there are six categories mentioned in the forty-sixth chapter, the "Chapter on Merits" (*Guṇavarga*).

First, the prophecy concerning the spiritual lineage (*gotra*); second, the prophecy concerning the initial arousal of the mind (*prathamacittotpāda*); third, the secret prophecy (*guhyavyākaraṇa*), which refers to those not seated in the assembly; fourth, the manifest prophecy (*sammukhavyākaraṇa*), which refers to those seated in the assembly;
fifth, that with a fixed limit; and sixth, that without a fixed limit. The reason only four are mentioned here is because the latter two are merely distinguished [by their temporal scope].
Regarding the time limit: it is no different from what preceded. Alternatively, there is a fourfold transmission difference.

The commentary states: this refers to those who produce [the path] through the middle grade of practice. The former was based on a five-part topical outline; this is based on a three-part topical outline.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the eight classes hear the name," as for those such as the nāgas, this is based on their past karma.
Now, examining the sutra text and its commentary, there is also the principle of an underlying intention regarding a different time. This sutra states that it is no different from what preceded;
how then could the nāgas and others be the same as before? Furthermore, if one says they are no different merely in terms of their birth, how could the nāgas and others possibly [be the same]?
Regarding birth in the Inner Court: if one were to speak thus based merely on a general rebirth there, it might be so insofar as it depends upon past karma;
yet even then, this would simply be equivalent to other gods of karmic retribution who are born there regardless of Maitreya—what connection, then, does this have to the present teaching?

Commentary: Regarding "firstly, not violating the precepts," this refers to possessing the precepts and not violating them; it is not the same as the inferior grade. This specific phrase does not appear in the sutra, yet according to the underlying principle, it is thus.
It does not say that violating the precepts constitutes non-violation. The subsequent phrase refers to those who have never received the precepts and do not commit evil.

Alternatively, the former phrase may mean possessing the precepts without violation, while the latter phrase implies that even if one were to violate them, it would not constitute a lack of discipline (*asaṃvara*). This is connected [to the following].

Next, regarding those whose offenses are minor: "evil" refers to the ten non-virtuous actions. The latter interpretation is superior. One who has not previously received the precepts will certainly be unable to be reborn in the Heaven of Contentment (Tuṣita).
